entries: You determine your available force or tech points by adding together the amount given by each class, but you only add your casting modifier once.
If you have both force and tech points, you keep your pools separate, and they can only be used to fuel force or {@book tech powers|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}, respectively.

entries.name: Max Power Level
entries: When multiclassing, you determine your Max Power Level by dividing each class's potential Max Power Level by 9, multiplying the result by the number of levels in that class, adding the results for each class together, and consulting the Multiclass Max Power Level table below.

For instance, if you have four levels in Marauder Approach berserker (1.77) and three levels in guardian (1.67), you count as a 3rd-level character when determining your Max Power Level, which is 2. While you don't know any 2nd-level powers, you can cast powers you know at that level.
If you have both force- and tech-casting, you determine your Max Power Levels separately, and they can only be used to cast force or {@book tech powers|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}, respectively.

entries.name: High-Level Casting
entries: When determining the number of higher level powers you can cast before needing a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, consult the rules for casting in the class in which you have the most levels.

entries.name: Feats
entries: A feat represents a talent or an area of {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} that gives character special capabilities. It embodies training, experience, and abilities beyond what a class provides. At certain levels, your class gives you the Ability Score Improvement feature. Using the optional feats rule, you can forgo taking that feature to take a feat of your choice instead. You can take each feat only once, unless the feat's description says otherwise.

You must meet any prerequisite specified in a feat to take that feat. If you ever lose a feat's prerequisite, you can't use that feat until you regain the prerequisite. For example, the {@feat Inspiring Leader|sw5e-phb} feat requires you to have a Charisma of 13 or higher. If your Charisma is reduced below 13 somehow—perhaps by a withering curse—you can't benefit from the {@feat Inspiring Leader|sw5e-phb} feat until your Charisma is restored.

entries.name: Fighting Styles
entries: Certain class features, or the {@feat Fighting Stylist|sw5e-phb} feat, offer your choice of fighting style. You can't choose a fighting style more than once, even if you later get to choose again.
You may choose your fighting style from the following options or roll on the table below to determine it randomly.

entries.name: Fighting Masteries
entries: Certain class features, or the {@feat Fighting Master|sw5e-phb} feat, offer your choice of fighting mastery. You can't choose a fighting mastery more than once, even if you later get to choose again.
You may choose your fighting mastery from the following options or roll on the table below to determine it randomly.

entries.name: Lightsaber Forms
entries: Certain class features, {@optfeature Formfighting Style|sw5e-phb}, or {@optfeature Formfighting Mastery|sw5e-phb}, offer your choice of {@book lightsaber forms|sw5e-phb|6|Lightsaber Forms}. You can't choose a {@book lightsaber form|sw5e-phb|6|Lightsaber Forms} more than once, even if you later get to choose again.
You may choose your {@book lightsaber forms|sw5e-phb|6|Lightsaber Forms} from the following options or roll on the table below to determine them randomly.
Each known form can be adopted on your turn by using your {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}.

data.name: Chapter 7: Using Ability Scores
entries: Six abilities provide a quick description of every creature's physical and mental characteristics: {@i _}

items: {@b Charisma}, measuring {@feat Force of Personality|sw5e-phb|force of personality}

entries: {@i _} Is a character muscle-bound and insightful? Brilliant and charming? Nimble and hardy? Ability scores define these qualities—a creature's assets as well as weaknesses.

The three main rolls of the game—the {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, and the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}—rely on the six ability scores. The book's introduction describes the basic rule behind these rolls: roll a {@dice d20}, add an ability modifier derived from one of the six ability scores, and compare the total to a target number.

This chapter focuses on how to use {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} and {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}, covering the fundamental activities that creatures attempt in the game. Rules for {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} appear in {@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9}.

entries.name: Ability Scores and Modifiers
entries: Each of a creature's abilities has a score, a number that defines the magnitude of that ability. An ability score is not just a measure of innate capabilities, but also encompasses a creature's training and competence in activities related to that ability.

A score of 10 or 11 is the normal human average, but adventurers and many monsters are a cut above average in most abilities. A score of 18 is the highest that a person usually reaches. Adventurers can have scores as high as 20, and monsters and villains can have scores as high as 30.

Each ability also has a modifier, derived from the score and ranging from -5 (for an ability score of 1) to +10 (for a score of 30). The Ability Scores and Modifiers table notes the ability modifiers for the range of possible ability scores, from 1 to 30.
To determine an ability modifier without consulting the table, subtract 10 from the ability score and then divide the total by 2 (round down).

Because ability modifiers affect almost every {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, and {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, ability modifiers come up in play more often than their associated scores.

entries.name: Advantage and Disadvantage
entries: Sometimes a special ability or power tells you that you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, or an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. When that happens, you roll a second {@dice d20} when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, and use the lower roll if you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}. For example, if you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} and roll a 17 and a 5, you use the 5. If you instead have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and roll those numbers, you use the 17.

entries.name: Ability Scores and Modifiers
entries: If multiple situations affect a roll and each one grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or imposes {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on it, you don't roll more than one additional {@dice d20}. If two favorable situations grant {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, for example, you still roll only one additional {@dice d20}.

If circumstances cause a roll to have both {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, you are considered to have neither of them, and you roll one {@dice d20}. This is true even if multiple circumstances impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} and only one grants {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or vice versa. In such a situation, you have neither {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} nor {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}.

When you make a roll with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, only the {@dice d20} is rolled twice. Any additional dice, such as the {@dice d4} granted by the {@i resistance} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, are only rolled once.

When you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} and something in the game, such as the iktotchi's Precognition trait, lets you reroll the {@dice d20}, you can reroll only one of the dice. You choose which one. For example, if an iktotchi has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} and rolls a 1 and a 13, the iktotchi could use the Precognition trait to reroll the 1.

You usually gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} through the use of special abilities, actions, or powers. {@book chapter 4|sw5e-phb|4}) can also give a character {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on checks related to the character's personality, ideals, or bonds. The GM can also decide that circumstances influence a roll in one direction or the other and grant {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} as a result.

entries.name: Advantage on Other Rolls
entries: Though less common, {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} can occur on other types of rolls as well. When you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on a roll, as with a {@dice d20}, you roll the dice twice, using the higher of the two results with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, and using the lower of the two results if you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}. If a roll has multiple dice, you roll the dice together and treat the results separately.

For instance, the second bullet of the {@feat Weapon Expert|sw5e-phb} feat grants conditional {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on a weapon's damage roll once per turn, provided you meet the criteria for that {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. If any additional dice would be added to the damage roll, such as the operative's Sneak Attack feature or the scout's Ranger's Quarry, those additional dice are only rolled once.

If granting {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on a roll that would have negative consequences rather than positive benefits, {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} should be reversed (as logic dictates). For instance, if a creature has a penalty die on a {@dice d20} roll, such as a {@dice d4} penalty die from the {@i denounce} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, and they get {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on that die roll, they should roll the {@dice d4} twice and take the higher roll, instead of the lower.

entries.name: Minimum Roll Threshold
entries: Certain features, such as the Great Weapon fighting style, add a minimum roll threshold, which means your dice can no longer roll below a certain amount, instead treating the die's result as the threshold. This threshold varies depending on the die size: 2 for {@dice d4}, 2 for {@dice d6}, 3 for {@dice d8}, 4 for {@dice d10}, 5 for {@dice d12}, and 8 for {@dice d20}.
For instance, a character with the Great Weapon fight style wielding a two-handed weapon that deals 1d12 rolls a 3 on a damage die, they treat the result as if they'd rolled a 5.

entries.name: Proficiency Bonus
entries: Characters have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} determined by level, as detailed in {@book chapter 1|sw5e-phb|1}. Monsters also have this bonus, which is incorporated in their stat blocks. The bonus is used in the rules on {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks}, {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}, and {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls}.

Your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} can't be added to a single die roll or other number more than once. For example, if two different rules say you can add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to a Wisdom {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, you nevertheless add the bonus only once when you make the save.

Occasionally, your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} might be multiplied or divided (doubled or halved. for example) before you apply it. If a circumstance suggests that your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} applies more than once to the same roll, you still add it only once and multiply or divide it only once.

By the same token, if a feature or effect allows you to multiply your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} when making an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} that wouldn't normally benefit from your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, you still don't add the bonus to the check. For that check your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} is 0, given the fact that multiplying 0 by any number is still 0. For instance, if you lack proficiency in the {@skill Lore|sw5e-phb} skill, you gain no benefit from a feature that lets you double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} when you make Intelligence ({@skill Lore|sw5e-phb}) checks.

In general, you don't multiply your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} for {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. If a feature or effect allows you to do so, these same rules apply.

entries.name: Expertise
entries: Certain features, such as the {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb} class feature or {@feat Ace Pilot|sw5e-phb} feat, grant {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill or tool, letting you double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} with that skill or tool. As usual, you can only gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill or tool once.

Far less common, though still possible, a creature can gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. Creatures cannot gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in weapons, however.

entries.name: Ability Checks
entries: An {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} tests a character's or monster's innate talent and training in an effort to overcome a challenge. The GM calls for an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} when a character or monster attempts an action (other than an attack) that has a chance of failure. When the outcome is uncertain, the dice determine the results.

For every {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, the GM decides which of the six abilities is relevant to the task at hand and the difficulty of the task, represented by Difficulty Class (DC). The more difficult a task, the higher its DC. The Ability Check DCs table shows common DCs.

To make an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, roll a {@dice d20} and add the relevant ability modifier. As with other {@dice d20} rolls, apply bonuses and penalties, and compare the total to the DC. If the total equals or exceeds the DC, the {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} is a success—the creature overcomes the challenge at hand. Otherwise, it's a failure, which means the character or monster makes no progress toward the objective or makes progress combined with a setback determined by the GM.

entries.name: Contests
entries: Sometimes one character's or monster's efforts are directly opposed to another's. This can occur when both of them are trying to do the same thing and only one can succeed, such as attempting to snatch up a ring that has fallen on the floor. This situation also applies when one of them is trying to prevent the other one from accomplishing a goal—for example, when a monster tries to force open a door that an adventurer is holding closed. In situations like these, the outcome is determined by a special form of {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, called a contest.

Both participants in a contest make {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} appropriate to their efforts. They apply all appropriate bonuses and penalties, but instead of comparing the total to a DC, they compare the totals of their two checks. The participant with the higher check total wins the contest. That character or monster either succeeds at the action or prevents the other one from succeeding.

If the contest results in a tie, the situation remains the same as it was before the contest. Thus, one contestant might win the contest by default. If two characters tie in a contest to snatch a ring off the floor, neither character grabs it. In a contest between a monster trying to open a door and an adventurer trying to keep the door closed, a tie means that the door remains shut.

entries.name: Additional Dice
entries: When making an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, some features grant an additional die when you make the {@dice d20} roll. If features would grant multiple additional dice in such a way, you can only benefit from one of them when you make the {@dice d20} roll (you choose which effect to use). For instance, if a creature is forced to make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, and it is benefiting from both a Potent Aptitude die and the {@i resistance} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, it can only use the additional die granted by one of those effects. Conversely, the same is true for penalty dice.

entries.name: Variant: Additional Die Teamwork
entries: In some instances, a party might be relying on the outcome made by a single party member's {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}. If multiple party members could grant that character an additional die, while that character couldn't apply multiple dice to the roll, you might consider allowing them to use the larger die provided, and to roll the die with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

entries.name: Multiple Modifiers
entries: As with additional dice, when making an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, some features might allow multiple modifiers being added to the roll. In these cases, only two modifiers may be added to a roll, and the same modifier can't be added twice unless an effect says so. For instance, if a friendly creature makes a Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} within range of a guardian's Aura of Presence, and that creature is also the target of a scholar's Critical Analysis, and they chose to end that Critical Analysis on themselves, they could add either that guardian's Wisdom modifier or the scholar's Intelligence modifier to their Constitution save, but not both.

entries.name: Applying During
entries: the {@dice d20} Roll Some features, such as engineer's Potent Aptitude or scholar's Critical Analysis, allow a creature to choose to add an additional die or ability modifier to an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. Unless the effect specifically says otherwise, it can be applied before or after the roll, but it must be applied before the GM determines whether the roll succeeds or fails.

entries.name: Skills
entries: Each ability covers a broad range of capabilities, including skills that a character or a monster can be proficient in. A skill represents a specific aspect of an ability score, and an individual's proficiency in a skill demonstrates a focus on that aspect.

The skills related to each ability score are shown in the following list. (No skills are related to Constitution.) See an ability's description in the later sections of this chapter for examples of how to use a skill associated with an ability.

items: {@b Dexterity}: {@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}, Sleight of Hand, {@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}
{@b Intelligence}: {@skill Investigation|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Lore|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Nature|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Piloting|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Technology|sw5e-phb}
{@b Wisdom}: Animal handling, {@skill Insight|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Medicine|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Survival|sw5e-phb}

entries: Sometimes, the GM might ask for an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} using a specific skill—for example, "Make a Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) check." At other times, a player might ask the GM if proficiency in a particular skill applies to a check. In either case, proficiency in a skill means an individual can add his or her {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} that involve that skill. Without proficiency in the skill, the individual makes a normal {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}.

For example, if a character attempts to climb up a dangerous cliff. the Dungeon Master might ask for a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check. If the character is proficient in {@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}, the character's {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} is added to the Strength check. If the character lacks that proficiency, he or she just makes a Strength check.

entries.name: Variant: Skills with Other Abilities
entries: Normally, your proficiency in a skill applies only to a specific kind of {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}. Proficiency in {@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}, for example, usually applies to Strength checks. In some situations, though, your proficiency might reasonably apply to a different kind of check. In such cases, the GM might ask for a check using an unusual combination of ability and skill, or you might ask your GM if you can apply a proficiency to a different check. For example, if you have to swim from an offshore island to the mainland, your GM might call for a Constitution check to see if you have the stamina to make it that far. In this case, your GM might allow you to apply your proficiency in {@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb} and ask for a Constitution ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check.

So if you're proficient in {@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}, you apply your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the Constitution check just as you would normally do for a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check. Similarly, when your trandoshan berserker uses a display of raw strength to intimidate an enemy, your GM might ask for a Strength ({@skill Intimidation|sw5e-phb}) check, even though {@skill Intimidation|sw5e-phb} is normally associated with Charisma.

entries.name: Passive Checks
entries: A passive check is a special kind of {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} that doesn't involve any die rolls. Such a check can represent the average result for a task done repeatedly, such as searching for secret doors over and over again, or can be used when the GM wants to secretly determine whether the characters succeed at something without rolling dice, such as noticing a hidden monster.

Here's how to determine a character's total for a passive check: 10 + all modifiers that normally apply to the check. If the character has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the check, add 5. For {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, subtract 5. The game refers to a passive check total as a score.
For example. if a 1st-level character has a Wisdom of 15 and proficiency in {@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}, he or she has a passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) score of 14.
The rules on hiding in the "Dexterity" section below rely on passive checks, as do the exploration rules in {@book chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8}.

entries.name: Working Together
entries: Sometimes two or more characters team up to attempt a task. The character who's leading the effort, or the one with the highest ability modifier, can make an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, reflecting the help provided by the other characters. In combat, this requires the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action (see {@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9}).

A character can only provide help if the task is one that he or she could attempt alone. For example, trying to open a lock requires proficiency with security kits, so a character who lacks that proficiency can't help another character in that task. Moreover. a character can help only when two or more individuals working together would actually be productive. Some tasks, such as threading a needle, are no easier with help.

entries.name: Group Checks
entries: When a number of individuals are trying to accomplish something together, the GM might ask for a group {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}. In such a situation, the characters who are skilled at the task at hand help {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} those who aren't. To make a group {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check},  everyone in the group makes the {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}. If at least half the group succeeds, the whole group succeeds. Otherwise, the group fails.

Group checks don't come up very often, and they're most useful when all the characters succeed or fail as a group. For example, when adventurers are navigating a swamp, the GM might call for a group Wisdom ({@skill Survival|sw5e-phb}) check to see if the characters can avoid the natural hazards of the environment. If at least half the group succeeds, the successful characters are able to guide their companions out of danger. Otherwise, the group stumbles into one of these hazards.

entries.name: Using Each Ability
entries: Every task that a character or monster might attempt in the game is covered by one of the six abilities. This section explains in more detail what those abilities mean and the ways they are used in the game.

entries.name: Strength
entries: Strength measures bodily power, athletic training, and the extent to which you can exert raw physical force.

entries.name: Strength Checks
entries: A Strength check can model any attempt to lift, push, pull, or break something, to force your body through a space, or to otherwise apply brute force to a situation. The {@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb} skill reflects aptitude in certain kinds of Strength checks.
{@b {@i Athletics.}} Your Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check covers difficult situations you encounter while climbing, jumping, or swimming. Examples include the following activities:

items: You attempt to climb a sheer or slippery cliff, avoid hazards while scaling a wall, or cling to a surface while something is trying to knock you off.
You try to jump an unusually long distance or pull off a stunt midjump.

You struggle to swim or stay afloat in treacherous currents, storm-tossed waves, or areas of thick seaweed. Or another creature tries to push or pull you underwater or otherwise interfere with your swimming.

entries: {@b {@i Other Strength Checks.}} The GM might also call for a Strength check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:

items: Force open a stuck, locked, or barred door
Push through a tunnel that is too small
Hang on to a wagon while being dragged behind it

entries.name: Attack Rolls and Damage
entries: You add your Strength modifier to your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} and your damage roll when attacking with a melee weapon such as a {@item Vibrosword|sw5e-phb|vibrosword} or {@item Doublesword|sw5e-phb|doublesword}. You use melee weapons to make melee attacks in hand—to—hand combat, and some of them can be thrown to make a ranged attack.

entries.name: Lifting and Carrying
entries: Your Strength score determines the amount of weight you can bear. The following terms define what you can lift or carry.

{@b {@i Carrying Capacity.}} Your carrying capacity is your Strength score multiplied by 15. This is the weight (in pounds) that you can carry, which is high enough that most characters don't usually have to worry about it.

{@b {@i Push, Drag, or Lift.}} You can push, drag, or lift a weight in pounds up to twice your carrying capacity (or 30 times your Strength score). While pushing or dragging weight in excess of your carrying capacity, your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} drops to 5 feet.

{@b {@i Size and Strength.}} Larger creatures can bear more weight, whereas Tiny creatures can carry less. For each size category above Medium, double the creature' carrying capacity and the amount it can push. drag, or lift. For a Tiny creature, halve these weights.

entries.name: Arm Equipment
entries: Certain equipment, such as a {@item Wristpad|sw5e-phb|wristpad}, light {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}, or fixed weapons, are worn on the forearm. A creature can only wield a number of such items on each forearm equal to half its Strength modifier (minimum of one item).

entries.name: Variant: Encumberance
entries: The rules for lifting and carrying are intentionally simple. Here is a variant if you are looking for more detailed rules for determining how a character is hindered by the weight of equipment. When you use this variant, ignore the Strength column of the Armor table in {@book chapter 5|sw5e-phb|5}.
If you carry weight in excess of 5 times your Strength score, you are {@b {@i encumbered}}, which means your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} drops by 10 feet.

If you carry weight in excess of 10 times your Strength score, up to your maximum carrying capacity, you are instead {@b {@i heavily encumbered}}, which means your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} drops by 20 feet and you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks}, {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls}, and {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} that use Strength, Dexterity, or Constitution.

entries.name: Dexterity
entries: Dexterity measures agility, reflexes, and balance.

entries.name: Dexterity Checks
entries: A Dexterity check can model any attempt to move nimbly, quickly, or quietly, or to keep from falling on tricky footing. The {@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}, Sleight of Hand, and {@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb} skills reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Dexterity checks.

{@b {@i Acrobatics.}} Your Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check covers your attempt to stay on your feet in a tricky situation, such as when you're trying to run across a sheet of ice, balance on a tightrope, or stay upright on a rocking spaceship's deck. The GM might also call for a Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check to see if you can perform acrobatic stunts, including dives, rolls, somersaults, and flips.

{@b {@i Sleight of Hand.}} Whenever you attempt an act of legerdemain or manual trickery, such as planting something on someone else or concealing an object on your person, make a Dexterity ({@skill Sleight Of Hand|sw5e-phb}) check. The GM might also call for a Dexterity ({@skill Sleight Of Hand|sw5e-phb}) check to determine whether you can lift a wallet off another person or slip something out of another person's pocket.

{@b {@i Stealth.}} Make a Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}) check when you attempt to conceal yourself from enemies, slink past guards, slip away without being noticed, or sneak up on someone without being seen or heard.
{@b {@i Other Dexterity Checks.}} The GM might call for a Dexterity check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:

items: Control a heavily laden cart on a steep descent
Steer a chariot around a tight turn
Craft a small or detailed object

entries.name: Attack Rolls and Damage
entries: You add your Dexterity modifier to your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} and your damage roll when attacking with a ranged weapon. such as a {@item Blaster rifle|sw5e-phb} or {@item Bowcaster|sw5e-phb|bowcaster}. You can also add your Dexterity modifier to your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} and your damage roll when attacking with a melee weapon that has {@itemProperty SWF|sw5e-phb|the finesse property}, such as a {@item Vibrodagger|sw5e-phb} or {@item Techblade|sw5e-phb}.

entries.name: Armor Class
entries: Depending on the armor you wear, you might add some or all of your Dexterity modifier to your {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb}, as described in {@book chapter 5|sw5e-phb|5}.

entries.name: Initiative
entries: At the beginning of every combat, you roll {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} by making a Dexterity check. {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb} determines the order of creatures' turns in combat, as described in {@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9}.

entries.name: Hiding
entries: hen you try to hide, make a Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}) check. Until you are discovered or you stop hiding, that checks total is contested by the Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) check of any creature that actively searches for signs of your presence. You can't hide from a creature that can see you, and if you make noise (such as shouting a warning or knocking over a vase), you give away your position. An {@condition Invisible|sw5e-phb|invisible} creature can't be seen, so it can always try to hide. Signs of its passage might still be noticed, however, and it still has to stay quiet. In combat, most creatures stay alert for signs of danger all around, so if you come out of hiding and approach a creature, it usually sees you. However, under certain circumstances, the Dungeon Master might allow you to stay hidden as you approach a creature that is distracted, allowing you to gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on an attack before you are seen. {@b {@i Passive Perception.}} When you hide, there's a chance someone will notice you even if they aren't searching. To determine whether such a creature notices you, the GM compares your Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}) check with that creature's passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) score, which equals 10 + the creature's Wisdom modifier, as well as any other bonuses or penalties. If the creature has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, add 5. For {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, subtract 5. For example, if a lst-level character (with a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2) has a Wisdom of 15 (a +2 modifier) and proficiency in {@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}, he or she has a passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) of 14. {@b {@i What Can You See?}} One of the main factors in determining whether you can find a hidden creature or object is how well you can see in an area, which might be {@b lightly} or {@b heavily} obscured, as explained in {@book chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8}.

entries.name: Constitution
entries: Constitution measures health, stamina, and vital force.

entries.name: Constitution Checks
entries: Constitution checks are uncommon, and no skills apply to Constitution checks. because the endurance this ability represents is largely passive rather than involving a specific effort on the part of a character or monster. A Constitution check can model your attempt to push beyond normal limits, however.
The GM might call for a Constitution check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:

items: March or labor for hours without rest
Quaff an entire stein of ale in one go

entries.name: Hit Points
entries: Your Constitution modifier contributes to your {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. Typically, you add your Constitution modifier to each Hit Die you roll for your {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.

If your Constitution modifier changes, your hit point maximum changes as well, as though you had the new modifier from 1st level. For example, if you raise your Constitution score when you reach 4th level and your Constitution modifier increases from +1 to +2, you adjust your hit point maximum as though the modifier had always been +2. So you add 3 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} for your first three levels, and then roll your {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} for 4th level using your new modifier. Or if you're 7th level and some effect lowers your Constitution score so as to reduce your Constitution modifier by 1, your hit point maximum is reduced by 7.

entries.name: Intelligence
entries: Intelligence measures mental acuity, accuracy of recall, and the ability to reason.

entries.name: Intelligence Checks
entries: An Intelligence check comes into play when you need to draw on logic, education, memory, or deductive reasoning. The {@skill Investigation|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Lore|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Nature|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Piloting|sw5e-phb}, and {@skill Technology|sw5e-phb} skills reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Intelligence checks.

{@b {@i Investigation.}} When you look around for clues and make deductions based on those clues, you make an Intelligence ({@skill Investigation|sw5e-phb}) check. You might deduce the location of a hidden object, discern from the appearance of a wound what kind of weapon dealt it, or determine the weakest point in a tunnel that could cause it to collapse. Poring through ancient materials in search of a hidden fragment of knowledge might also call for an Intelligence ({@skill Investigation|sw5e-phb}) check.
{@b {@i Lore.}} Your Intelligence ({@skill Lore|sw5e-phb}) check measures your ability to recall information about the Force, artifacts, histories, and religions.
{@b {@i Nature.}} Your Intelligence ({@skill Nature|sw5e-phb}) check measures your ability to recall lore about terrain, plants and animals, the weather, and natural cycles.

{@b {@i Piloting.}} Your Intelligence ({@skill Piloting|sw5e-phb}) check measures your ability to control vehicles, aircraft, and spaceships. {@skill Piloting|sw5e-phb} governs your ability to maneuver through tight spaces and debris fields or dogfight with enemy craft.

{@b {@i Technology.}} Your Intelligence ({@skill Technology|sw5e-phb}) checks measure your ability to recall information about droids, vehicles, spaceships, aircraft, and computers, as well as your ability to interface with them. {@skill Technology|sw5e-phb} can also be used to stabilize a droid or construct.
{@b {@i Other Intelligence Checks.}} The GM might call for an Intelligence check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:

items: Communicate with a creature without using words
Estimate the value of a precious item
Pull together a disguise to pass as a city guard
Recall lore about a craft or trade

entries.name: Force- and Tech-casting Ability
entries: Techcasters use Intelligence as their {@book techcasting ability|sw5e-phb|10|Techcasting Ability}, which helps determine the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} DCs of power they cast.

entries.name: Wisdom
entries: Wisdom reflects how attuned you are to the world around you and represents perceptiveness and intuition.

entries.name: Wisdom Checks
entries: A Wisdom check might reflect an effort to read body language, understand someone's feelings, notice things about the environment, or care for an injured person. The {@skill Animal Handling|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Insight|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Medicine|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}, and {@skill Survival|sw5e-phb} skills reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Wisdom checks.

{@b {@i Animal Handling.}} When there is any question whether you can calm down a domesticated animal, keep a mount from getting spooked, or intuit an animal's intentions, the GM might call for a Wisdom ({@skill Animal Handling|sw5e-phb}) check. You also make a Wisdom ({@skill Animal Handling|sw5e-phb}) check to control your mount when you attempt a risky maneuver.

{@b {@i Insight.}} Your Wisdom ({@skill Insight|sw5e-phb}) check decides whether you can determine the true intentions of a creature, such as when searching out a lie or predicting someone's next move. Doing so involves gleaning clues from body language, speech habits, and changes in mannerisms.
{@b {@i Medicine.}} A Wisdom ({@skill Medicine|sw5e-phb}) check lets you try to stabilize a dying companion or diagnose an illness.

{@b {@i Perception.}} Your Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) check lets you spot, hear, or otherwise detect the presence of something. It measures your general awareness of your surroundings and the keenness of your senses. For example, you might try to hear a conversation through a closed door, eavesdrop under an open window, or hear monsters moving stealthily in the forest. Or you might try to spot things that are obscured or easy to miss, whether they are orcs lying in ambush on a road, thugs hiding in the shadows of an alley, or candlelight under a closed secret door.

{@b {@i Survival.}} The GM might ask you to make a Wisdom ({@skill Survival|sw5e-phb}) check to follow tracks, hunt wild game, guide your group through frozen wastelands, identify signs that rancors live nearby, predict the weather, or avoid quicksand and other natural hazards.
{@b {@i Other Wisdom Checks.}} The GM might call for a Wisdom check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:

items: Get a gut feeling about what course of action to follow
Discern Whether a seemingly dead or living creature is undead

entries.name: Force- and Tech-casting Ability
entries: Forcecasters use Wisdom as their {@book forcecasting ability|sw5e-phb|10|Forcecasting Ability} for their light side and {@book universal powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, which helps determine the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} DCs of powers they cast.

entries.name: Finding a Hidden Object
entries: When your character searches for a hidden object such as a secret door or a trap, the GM typically asks you to make a Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) check. Such a check can be used to find hidden details or other information and clues that you might otherwise overlook. In most cases, you need to describe where you are looking in order for the GM to determine your chance of success. For example, a key is hidden beneath a set of folded clothes in the top drawer ofa bureau. If you tell the GM that you pace around the room, looking at the walls and furniture for clues, you have no chance of finding the key, regardless of your Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) check result. You would have to specify that you were opening the drawers or searching the bureau in order to have any chance of success.

entries.name: Charisma
entries: Charisma measures your ability to interact effectively with others. It includes such factors as confidence and eloquence, and it can represent a charming or commanding personality.

entries.name: Charisma Checks
entries: A Charisma check might arise when you try to influence or entertain others, when you try to make an impression or tell a convincing lie, or when you are navigating a tricky social situation. The {@skill Deception|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Intimidation|sw5e-phb}, {@skill Performance|sw5e-phb}, and {@skill Persuasion|sw5e-phb} skills reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Charisma checks.

{@b {@i Deception.}} Your Charisma ({@skill Deception|sw5e-phb}) check determines whether you can convincingly hide the truth, either verbally or through your actions. This deception can encompass everything from misleading others through ambiguity to telling outright lies. Typical situations include trying to fast-talk a guard, con a merchant, earn money through gambling, pass yourself off in a disguise, dull someone's suspicions with false assurances, or maintain a straight face while telling a blatant lie.

{@b {@i Intimidation.}} When you attempt to influence someone through overt threats, hostile actions, and physical violence, the GM might ask you to make a Charisma ({@skill Intimidation|sw5e-phb}) check. Examples include trying to pry information out of a prisoner, convincing street thugs to back down from a confrontation, or using the edge of a broken {@item Bottle|sw5e-phb|bottle} to convince a sneering vizier to reconsider a decision.

{@b {@i Performance.}} Your Charisma ({@skill Performance|sw5e-phb}) check determines how well you can delight an audience with music, dance. acting, storytelling, or some other form of entertainment.

{@b {@i Persuasion.}} When you attempt to influence someone or a group of people with tact, social graces, or good nature, the GM might ask you to make a Charisma ({@skill Persuasion|sw5e-phb}) check. Typically, you use persuasion when acting in good faith, to foster friendships, make cordial requests, or exhibit proper etiquette. Examples of persuading others include convincing a Chamberlain to let your party see the king, negotiating peace between warring tribes, or inspiring a crowd of townsfolk.
{@b {@i Other Charisma Checks.}} The GM might call for a Charisma check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:

items: Find the best person to talk to for news, rumors, and gossip
Blend into a crowd to get the sense of key topics of conversation

entries.name: Force- and Tech-casting Ability
entries: Forcecasters use Charisma as their {@book forcecasting ability|sw5e-phb|10|Forcecasting Ability} for their dark side and {@book universal powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, which helps determine the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} DCs of powers they cast.

entries.name: Saving Throws
entries: A {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}-also called a save-represents an attempt to resist a power, a trap, a poison, a disease, or a similar threat. You don't normally decide to make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}; you are forced to make one because your character or monster is at risk of harm.

To make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, roll a {@dice d20} and add the appropriate ability modifier. For example, you use your Dexterity modifier for a Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}.

A {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} can be modified by a situational bonus or penalty and can be affected by {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, as determined by the GM.

Each class gives proficiency in at least two {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. The operative, for example, is proficient in Intelligence saves. As with skill proficiencies, proficiency in a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} lets a character add his or her {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} made using a particular ability score. Some monsters have {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} proficiencies as well.

The Difficulty Class for a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} is determined by the effect that causes it. For example, the DC for a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} allowed by a power is determined by the caster's force- or tech-casting ability and {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

The result of a successful or failed {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} is also detailed in the effect that allows the save. Usually, a successful save means that a creature suffers no harm, or reduced harm, from an effect.

data.name: Chapter 8: Adventuring
entries: Delving into an ancient Sith tomb, slipping through the Black Sun territory of Coruscant, hacking a fresh trail through the thick jungles on the forest moon of Endor—these are the things that {@i Star Wars} adventures are made of. Your character in the game might explore forgotten ruins and uncharted lands, uncover dark secrets and sinister plots, and slay foul monsters. And if all goes well, your character will survive to claim rich rewards before embarking on a new adventure.

This chapter covers the basics of the adventuring life, from the mechanics of movement to the complexities of social interaction. The rules for resting are also in this chapter, along with a discussion of the activities your character might pursue between adventures.

Whether adventurers are exploring a dusty dungeon or the complex relationships of a noble court, the game follows a natural rhythm, as outlined in the book's introduction: {@b {@i  {@b 1. The GM describes the environment.} {@b 2. The players describe what they want to do.} {@b 3. The GM narrates the results of their actions.} }} Typically, the GM uses a map as an outline of the adventure, tracking the characters' progress as they explore enclave corridors or wilderness regions.

The GM's notes, including a key to the map, describe what the adventurers find as they enter each new area. Sometimes, the passage of time and the adventurers' actions determine what happens, so the GM might use a timeline or a flowchart to track their progress instead of a map.

entries.name: Time
entries: In situations where keeping track of the passage of time is important, the GM determines the time a task requires. The GM might use a different time scale depending on the context of the situation at hand. In an enclosed environment, the adventurers' movement happens on a scale of minutes. It takes them about a minute to creep down a long hallway, another minute to check for traps on the door at the end of the hall, and a good ten minutes to search the chamber beyond for anything interesting or valuable.

In a city or wilderness, a scale of hours is often more appropriate. Adventurers eager to reach the lonely tower at the heart of the forest hurry across those fifteen miles in just under four hours time.
For long journeys, a scale of days works best. Following the road from Tatooine to Kashyyk, the adventurers spend four uneventful days before a pirate ambush interrupts their journey.
In combat and other fast-paced situations, the game relies on rounds, a 6-second span of time described in {@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9}.

entries.name: Movement
entries: Swimming across a rushing river, sneaking down a building corridor, scaling a treacherous mountain slope- all sorts of movement play a key role in D&D adventures.

The GM can summarize the adventurers' movement without calculating exact distances or travel times: "You travel through the forest and find the ruin entrance late in the evening of the third day." Even in a dungeon, particularly a large dungeon or a cave network, the GM can summarize movement between encounters: "After killing the guardian at the entrance to the ancient Jedi stronghold. you consult your map, which leads you through miles of echoing corridors to a chasm bridged by a narrow stone arch."

Sometimes it's important, though, to know how long it takes to get from one spot to another, whether the answer is in days, hours, or minutes. The rules for determining travel time depend on two factors: the {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} and travel pace of the creatures moving and the terrain they're moving over.

entries.name: Speed
entries: Every character and monster has a {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}, which is the distance in feet that the character or monster can walk in 1 round. This number assumes short bursts of energetic movement in the midst of a life-threatening situation.
The following rules determine how far a character or monster can move in a minute, an hour, or a day.

entries.name: Travel Pace
entries: While traveling, a group of adventurers can move at a normal, fast, or slow pace, as shown on the Travel Pace table. The table states how far the party can move in a period of time and whether the pace has any effect. A fast pace makes characters less perceptive, while a slow pace makes it possible to sneak around and to search an area more carefully (see the {@book Activity While Traveling|sw5e-phb|8|Activity While Traveling} section later in this chapter for more information).
{@b {@i Forced March.}} The Travel Pace table assumes that characters travel for 8 hours in day. They can push on beyond that limit, at the risk of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}.

For each additional hour of travel beyond 8 hours, the characters {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} the distance shown in the Hour column for their pace, and each character must make a Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} at the end of the hour. The DC is 10 + 1 for each hour past 8 hours. On a failed {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, a character suffers one level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} (see {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}).

{@b {@i Mounts, Speeders, and Vehicles.}} For short spans of time (up to an hour), many animals move much faster than humanoids. A mounted character can ride at a gallop for about an hour, covering twice the usual distance for a fast pace. If fresh mounts are available every 8 to 10 miles, characters can {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} larger distances at this pace, but this is very rare except in densely populated areas.
Characters in shuttles, speeders, or other vehicles choose a pace as normal. Depending on the vessel and the size of the crew, ships might be able to travel for up to 24 hours per day.

rows: -5 penalty to passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) scores

entries.name: Difficult Terrain
entries: The travel speeds given in the Travel Pace table assume relatively simple terrain: roads, open plains, or clear enclosed corridors. But adventurers often face dense forests, deep swamps, rubble-filled ruins, steep mountains, and ice-covered ground—all considered {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

You move at half {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} in {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}—moving 1 foot in {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain} costs 2 feet of {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}—so you can {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} only half the normal distance in a minute, an hour, or a day.

entries.name: Special Types of Movement
entries: Movement through dangerous dungeons or wilderness areas often involves more than simply walking. Adventurers might have to climb, crawl, swim, or jump to get where they need to go.

entries.name: Climbing, Swimming and Crawling
entries: While climbing, swimming, or crawling, each foot of movement costs 1 extra foot (2 extra feet in {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}), unless a creature has a climbing or swimming {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. At the GM's option, climbing a slippery vertical surface or one with few handholds requires a successful Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check. Similarly, gaining any distance in rough water might require a successful Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check.

entries.name: Jumping
entries: Your Strength determines how far you can jump.

{@b {@i Long Jump.}} When you make a long jump, you {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} a number of feet up to your Strength score if you move at least 10 feet on foot immediately before the jump. When you make a standing long jump, you can leap only half that distance. Either way, each foot you clear on the jump costs a foot of movement.

This rule assumes that the height of your jump doesn't matter, such as a jump across a stream or chasm. At your GM's option, you must succeed on a DC 10 Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check to clear a low obstacle (no taller than a quarter of the jump's distance), such as a hedge or low wall. Otherwise, you hit it.

When you land in {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}, you must succeed on a DC 10 Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check to land on your feet. Otherwise, you land prone.

{@b {@i High Jump.}} When you make a high jump, you leap into the air a number of feet equal to 3 + your Strength modifier if you move at least 10 feet on foot immediately before the jump. When you make a standing high jump, you can jump only half that distance. Either way, each foot you clear on the jump costs a foot of movement. In some circumstances, your GM might allow you to make a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check to jump higher than you normally can.
You can extend your arms half your height above yourself during the jump. Thus, you can reach above you a distance equal to the height of the jump plus 1 1/2 times your height.

entries.name: Activity While Traveling
entries: As adventurers travel through a dungeon or the wilderness, they need to remain alert for danger, and some characters might perform other tasks to help the group's journey.

entries.name: Marching Order
entries: The adventurers should establish a marching order.
A marching order makes it easier to determine which characters are affected by traps, which ones can spot hidden enemies, and which ones are the closest to those enemies when a fight breaks out.

A character might occupy the front rank, one or more middle ranks, or the back rank. Characters in the front and back ranks need enough room to travel side by side with others in their rank. When space is too tight, the marching order must change, usually by moving characters to a middle rank.

{@b {@i Fewer Than Three Ranks.}} If an adventuring party arranges its marching order with only two ranks, they are a front rank and a back rank. If there's only one rank, it's considered a front rank.

entries.name: Stealth
entries: While traveling at a slow pace, the characters can move stealthily. As long as they're not in the open, they can try to surprise or sneak by other creatures they encounter. See the rules for hiding in {@book chapter 7|sw5e-phb|7}.

entries.name: Noticing Threats
entries: Use the passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) scores of the characters to determine whether anyone in the group notices a hidden threat. The GM might decide that a threat can be noticed only by characters in a particular rank. For example, as the characters are exploring a maze of tunnels, the GM might decide that only those characters in the back rank have a chance to hear or spot a stealthy creature following the group, while characters in the front and middle ranks cannot. While traveling at a fast pace, characters take a -5 penalty to their passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) scores to notice hidden threats.

{@b {@i Encountering Creatures.}} If the GM determines that the adventurers encounter other creatures while they're traveling, it's up to both groups to decide what happens next. Either group might decide to attack, initiate a conversation, run away, or wait to see what the other group does.

{@b {@i Surprising Foes.}} If the adventurers encounter a hostile creature or group, the GM determines whether the adventurers or their foes might be surprised when combat erupts. See {@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9} for more about surprise.

entries.name: Other Activities
entries: Characters who turn their attention to other tasks as the group travels are not focused on watching for danger. These characters don't contribute their passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) scores to the group's chance of noticing hidden threats. However, a character not watching for danger can do one of the following activities instead, or some other activity with the GM's permission.

{@b {@i Navigate.}} The character can try to prevent the group from becoming lost, making a Wisdom ({@skill Survival|sw5e-phb}) check when the GM calls for it. (The {@i Dungeon Master's Guide} has rules to determine whether the group gets lost.)

{@b {@i Draw a Map.}} The character can draw a map that records the group's progress and helps the characters get back on course if they get lost. No {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} is required.

{@b {@i Track.}} A character can follow the tracks of another creature, making a Wisdom ({@skill Survival|sw5e-phb}) check when the GM calls for it. (The {@i Dungeon Master's Guide} has rules for tracking.)

{@b {@i Forage.}} The character can keep an eye out for ready sources of food and water, making a Wisdom ({@skill Survival|sw5e-phb}) check when the GM calls for it. (The {@i Dungeon Master's Guide} has rules for foraging.)

entries.name: Splitting Up
entries: the Party Sometimes, it makes sense to split an adventuring party, especially if you want one or more characters to scout ahead. You can form multiple parties, each moving at a different {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. Each group has its own front, middle, and back ranks. The drawback to this approach is that the party will be split into several smaller groups in the event of an attack. The {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} is that a small group of stealthy characters moving slowly might be able to sneak past enemies that clumsier characters would alert. An operative and a monk moving at a slow pace are much harder to detect when they leave their guardian friend behind.

entries.name: The Environment
entries: By its nature, adventuring involves delving into places that are dark, dangerous, and full of mysteries to be explored. The rules in this section {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} some of the most important ways in which adventurers interact with the environment in such places. The Dungeon Master's Guide has rules covering more unusual situations.

entries.name: Falling
entries: A fall from a great height is one of the most common hazards facing an adventurer.
At the end of a fall, a creature takes 1d6 kinetic damage for every 10 feet it fell, to a maximum of 20d6. The creature lands prone, unless it avoids taking damage from the fall.

entries.name: Suffocating
entries: A creature can hold its breath for a number of minutes equal to 1 + its Constitution modifier (minimum of 30 seconds). When a creature runs out of breath, it can survive for a number of rounds equal to its Constitution modifier (minimum 1 round). At the start of its next turn, it drops to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and is dying.

entries.name: High and Low Pressure Environs
entries: If a creature is exposed a high or low pressure environ such as the vacuum of space or the deep ocean, it can survive for a number of rounds equal to its Constitution modifier (minimum 1 round). At the start of its next turn, it immediately dies without making {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throws}.

entries.name: Vision and Light
entries: The most fundamental tasks of adventuring—noticing danger, finding hidden objects, hitting an enemy in combat, and targeting a power, to name just a few—rely heavily on a character's ability to see. darkness and other effects that obscure vision can prove a significant hindrance.

A given area might be lightly or heavily obscured. In a {@b lightly obscured} area, such as dim light, patchy fog, or moderate foliage, creatures have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) checks that rely on sight.

A {@b heavily obscured} area-such as darkness, opaque fog, or dense foliage-blocks vision entirely. A creature in or looking in a heavily obscured area effectively suffers from the {@condition Blinded|sw5e-phb|blinded} condition (see {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}).
The presence or absence of light in an environment creates three categories of illumination: bright light, dim light, and darkness.
{@b Bright light} lets most creatures see normally. Even gloomy days provide bright light, as do torches, lanterns, fires, and other sources of illumination within a specific radius.

{@b Dim light}, also called shadows, creates a lightly obscured area. An area of dim light is usually a boundary between a source of bright light, such as a torch, and surrounding darkness. The soft light of twilight and dawn also counts as dim light. A particularly brilliant full moon might bathe the land in dim light.
{@b Darkness} creates a heavily obscured area. Characters face darkness outdoors at night (even most moonlit nights), or within the confines of an unlit dungeon or a subterranean vault.

entries.name: Blindsight
entries: A creature with {@sense Blindsight|sw5e-phb|blindsight} can perceive its surroundings without relying on sight, within a specific radius. Creatures without eyes, such as Miraluka, and creatures with echolocation or heightened senses, such as Togruta or Verpine, have this sense.

entries.name: Darkvision
entries: Many creatures in the worlds of Star Wars, especially those that dwell underground, have {@sense Darkvision|sw5e-phb|darkvision}. Within a specified range, a creature with {@sense Darkvision|sw5e-phb|darkvision} can see in darkness as if the darkness were dim light, so areas of darkness are only lightly obscured as far as that creature is concerned. However, the creature can't discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.

entries.name: Truesight
entries: A creature with {@sense Truesight|sw5e-phb|truesight} can, out to a specific range, see in normal and enhanced darkness, see {@condition Invisible|sw5e-phb|invisible} creatures and objects, automatically detect visual illusions and succeed on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against them, and perceives the original form of a shapechanger or a creature that is transformed by a power.

entries.name: Food and Water
entries: Characters who don't eat or drink suffer the effects of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} (see {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}). {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb} caused by lack of food or water can't be removed until the character eats and drinks the full required amount.

entries.name: Food
entries: A character needs one pound of food per day and can make food last longer by subsisting on half rations. Eating half a pound of food in a day counts as half a day without food. A character can go without food for a number of days equal to 3 + his or her Constitution modifier (minimum 1). At the end of each day beyond that limit, a character automatically suffers one level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}. A normal day of eating resets the count of days without food to zero.

entries.name: Water
entries: A character needs one gallon of water per day, or two gallons per day if the weather is hot. A character who drinks only half that much water must succeed on a DC 15 Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} or suffer one level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} at the end of the day. A character with access to less water automatically suffers one level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} at the end of the day. If the character already has one or more levels of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}, the character takes two levels in either case.

entries.name: Interacting with Objects
entries: A character's interaction with objects in an environment is often simple to resolve in the game. The player tells the GM that his or her character is doing something, such a moving a lever, and the GM describes what, if anything happens. For example, a character might decide to pull a lever, which might, in turn, open a door, cause a room to flood with water, or open a secret door in a nearby wall. If the lever is rusted in position, though, a character might need to force it. In such a situation, the GM might call for a Strength check to see whether the character can wrench the lever into place. The GM sets the DC for any such check based on the difficulty of the task.

Characters can also damage objects with their weapons and powers. Objects are immune to necrotic, poison, and psychic damage, but otherwise they can be affected by physical attacks and powers much like creatures can. Generally, objects are immune to any conditions that are illogical, such as {@condition Charmed|sw5e-phb|charmed} or {@condition Frightened|sw5e-phb}. The GM determines an object's {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb} and {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, and might decide that certain objects have resistance or immunity to certain kinds of attacks. (It's hard to cut a rope with a club, for example.) Objects always fail Strength, Dexterity, and Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}, and they are immune to effects that require other saves. When an object drops to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, it breaks. A character can also attempt a Strength check to break an object. The GM sets the DC for any such check.

entries.name: Social Interaction
entries: Exploring dungeons, overcoming obstacles, and slaying monsters are key parts of D&D adventures. No less important, though, are the social interactions that adventurers have with other inhabitants of the world.

Interaction takes on many forms. You might need to convince an unscrupulous thief to confess to some malfeasance, or you might try to flatter a Hutt so that he will spare your life. The GM assumes the roles of any characters who are participating in the interaction that don"t belong to another player at the table. Any such character is called a {@b nonplayer character} (NPC).

In general terms, an NPC's attitude toward you is described as friendly, indifferent, or hostile. Friendly NPCs are predisposed to help you, and hostile ones are inclined to get in your way. It's easier to get what you want from a friendly NPC, of course.
Social interactions have two primary aspects: roleplaying and {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks}.

entries.name: Roleplaying
entries: Roleplaying is, literally, the act of playing out a role. In this case, it's {@i you} as a player determining how your character thinks, acts, and talks.
Roleplaying is a part of every aspect of the game, and it comes to the fore during social interactions. Your character's quirks, mannerisms, and personality influence how interactions resolve.

There are two styles you can use when roleplaying your character: the descriptive approach and the active approach. Most players use a combination of the two styles. Use whichever mix of the two works best for you.

entries.name: Descriptive Approach to Roleplaying
entries: With this approach. you describe your character's words and actions to the GM and the other players. Drawing on your mental image of your character, you tell everyone what your character does and how he or she does it.

For instance, Chris plays Tordek the Nikto. Tordek has a quick temper and blames the Black Sun for his family's misfortune. At a bar, an obnoxious Twi'lek operative sits at Tordek's table and tries to strike up a conversation with the Nikto.
Chris says, "Tordek spits on the floor, growls an insult at the Twi'lek, and stomps over to the bar. He sits on a stool and glares at the operative before ordering another drink."
In this example, Chris has conveyed Tordek's mood and given the GM a clear idea of his characters attitude and actions.
When using descriptive roleplaying, keep the following things in mind:

items: Describe your character's emotions and attitude.
Focus on your character's intent and how others might perceive it.
Provide as much embellishment as you feel comfortable with.

entries: Don't worry about getting things exactly right. Just focus on thinking about what your character would do and describing what you see in your mind.

entries.name: Active Approach to Roleplaying
entries: If descriptive roleplaying tells your GM and your fellow players what your character thinks and does, active roleplaying {@i shows} them.

When you use active roleplaying, you speak with your character's voice, like an actor taking on a role. You might even echo your character's movements and body language. This approach is more immersive than descriptive roleplaying, though you still need to describe things that can't be reasonably acted out.

Going back to the example of Chris roleplaying Tordek above, here's how the scene might play out if Chris used active roleplaying: Speaking as Tordek, Chris says in a gruff, deep voice, "I was wondering why it suddenly smelled awful in here. If I wanted to hear anything out of you, I'd snap your arm and enjoy your screams." In his normal voice. Chris then adds, "I get up, glare at the Twi'lek, and head to the bar."

entries.name: Results of Roleplaying
entries: The GM uses your character's actions and attitudes to determine how an NPC reacts. A cowardly NPC buckles under threats of violence. A stubborn Jawa refuses to let anyone badger her. A vain Hutt laps up flattery.

When interacting with an NPC, pay close attention to the GM's portrayal ofthe NPC's mood, dialogue, and personality. You might be able to determine an NPC's personality traits, ideals, flaws, and bonds, then play on them to influence the NPC's attitude.

Interactions in D&D are much like interactions in real life. If you can offer NPCS something they want, threaten them with something they fear, or play on their sympathies and goals, you can use words to get almost anything you want. On the other hand, if you insult a proud warrior or speak ill of a senator's allies, your efforts to convince or {@optfeature Deceive|sw5e-phb|deceive} will fall short.

entries.name: Ability Checks
entries: In addition to roleplaying, {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} are key in determining the outcome of an interaction.

Your roleplaying efforts can alter an NPC's attitude, but there might still be an element of chance in the situation. For example, your GM can call for a Charisma check at any point during an interaction if he or she wants the dice to play a role in determining an NPC's reactions. Other checks might be appropriate in certain situations, at your GM's discretion.

Pay attention to your skill proficiencies when thinking of how you want to interact with an NPC, and {@spell Stack the Deck|sw5e-phb|stack the deck} in your favor by using an approach that relies on your best bonuses and skills. If the group needs to trick a guard into letting them into a pavilion, the scoundrel who is proficient in {@skill Deception|sw5e-phb} is the best bet to lead the discussion. When negotiating for a hostage's release, the force initiate with {@skill Persuasion|sw5e-phb} should do most of the talking.

entries.name: Resting
entries: Heroic though they might be, adventurers can't spend every hour of the day in the thick of exploration, social interaction, and combat. They need rest time to sleep and eat, tend their wounds, refresh their batteries and spirits for force- and tech-casting, and brace themselves for further adventure.
Adventurers can take short rests in the midst of an adventuring day and a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} to end the day.

entries.name: Short Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} is a period of downtime, at least 1 hour long, during which a character does nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, and tending to wounds.

A character can spend one or more Hit Dice at the end of a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest}, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's level. Whenever a character spends a Hit Die to regain {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.

entries.name: Long Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} is a period of extended downtime, at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps for at least 6 hours and performs light activity, such as reading, talking, eating, or standing watch, for no more than 2 hours. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity—fighting, casting powers, at least 1 hour of walking, or similar adventuring activity—the characters must restart the rest to benefit from it.

At the end of a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, a character regains all lost {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them (minimum of one).

A character can't benefit from more than one {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

entries.name: Variant: Resting in Armor
entries: Resting in armor makes it difficult to recover fully. At the end of a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, if you wore your armor, you only recover one-quarter your spent Hit Dice (minimum of one), instead of half.

entries.name: Between Adventures
entries: Between trips to dungeons and battles against ancient evils, adventurers need time to rest, recuperate, and prepare for their next adventure. Many adventurers also use this time to perform other tasks, such as crafting arms and armor, gambling, or spending their hard-earned credits.

In some cases, the passage of time is something that occurs with little fanfare or description. When starting a new adventure, the GM might simply declare that a certain amount of time has passed and allow you to describe in general terms what your character has been doing. At other times, the GM might want to keep track of just how much time is passing as events beyond your perception stay in motion.

entries.name: Lifestyle Expenses
entries: Between adventures, you choose a particular quality of life and pay the cost of maintaining that lifestyle, as described in {@book chapter 5|sw5e-phb|5}.

Living a particular lifestyle doesn't have a huge effect on your character, but your lifestyle can affect the way other individuals and groups react to you. For example, when you lead an aristocratic lifestyle, it might be easier for you to influence the nobles of the city than if you live in poverty.

entries.name: Downtime Activities
entries: Between adventures, the GM might ask you what your character is doing during his or her downtime. Periods of downtime can vary in duration, but each downtime activity requires a certain number of days to complete before you gain any benefit, and at least 8 hours of each day must be spent on the downtime activity for the day to count. The days do not need to be consecutive. If you have more than the minimum amount of days to spend, you can keep doing the same thing for a longer period of time, or switch to a new downtime activity.
Downtime activities other than the ones presented below are possible. If you want your character to spend his or her downtime performing an activity not covered here, discuss it with your GM.

entries.name: Crafting
entries: You can craft unenhanced objects, including adventuring equipment and works of art. While you don't need to be proficient with tools related to the object you are trying to create (typically artisan's implements), without proficiency you will lack the knowledge of what objects you can create. You might also need access to special materials or locations necessary to create it. For example, someone proficient with {@item Armstech's implements|sw5e-phb|armstech's implements} needs a workstation in order to craft a {@item Vibrosword|sw5e-phb|vibrosword}.

For every day of downtime you spend crafting, you can craft one or more items with a total market value not exceeding 250 cr, and you must expend raw materials worth half the total market value.
