If something you want to craft has a market value greater than 250 cr, you make progress every day in 250-cr increments until you reach the market value of the item. For example, a {@item Heavy exoskeleton|sw5e-phb|heavy exoskeleton} (market value 9,000 cr) takes 36 days to craft by yourself, at a total cost of 4,500 cr.

Multiple characters can combine their efforts toward the crafting of a single item, provided that the characters all have proficiency with the requisite tools and are working together in the same place. Each character contributes 250 cr worth of effort for every day spent helping to craft the item. For example, three characters with the requisite tool proficiency and the proper facilities can craft a {@item Heavy exoskeleton|sw5e-phb|heavy exoskeleton} in 12 days, at a total cost of 4,500 cr.

While crafting, you can maintain a modest lifestyle, as discussed in {@book chapter 5|sw5e-phb|5}, without having to pay 10 cr per day. If you have {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in your chosen tool, you can instead maintain a comfortable lifestyle without having to pay 20 cr per day.

entries.name: Practicing a Profession
entries: You can work between adventures, allowing you to maintain a modest lifestyle without having to pay 10 cr per day (see {@book chapter 5|sw5e-phb|5} for more information on lifestyle expenses). This benefit lasts as long you continue to practice your profession.
If you are a member of an organization that can provide gainful employment, such as a syndicate or guild, you earn enough to support a comfortable lifestyle instead.
If you have proficiency in the {@skill Performance|sw5e-phb} skill and put your performance skill to use during your downtime, you earn enough to support a wealthy lifestyle instead.

entries.name: Recuperating
entries: You can use downtime between adventures to recover from a debilitating injury, disease, or poison.

After three days of downtime spent recuperating, you can make a DC 15 Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. On a successful save, you can choose one of the following results:

items: End one effect on you that prevents you from regaining {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.
For the next 24 hours, gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against one disease or poison currently affecting you.

entries.name: Researching
entries: The time between adventures is a great chance to perform research, gaining insight into mysteries that have unfurled over the course of the campaign. Research can include poring over dusty tomes and ancient datacrons in a library or buying drinks for the locals to pry rumors and gossip from their lips.

When you begin your research, the GM determines whether the information is available, how many days of downtime it will take to find it, and whether there are any restrictions on your research (such as needing to seek out a specific individual, tome, or location). The GM might also require you to make one or more {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks}, such as an Intelligence ({@skill Investigation|sw5e-phb}) check to find clues pointing toward the information you seek, or a Charisma ({@skill Persuasion|sw5e-phb}) check to secure someone's aid. Once those conditions are met, you learn the information if it is available.

For each day of research, you must spend 10 cr to {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} your expenses. This cost is in addition to your normal lifestyle expenses (as discussed in {@book chapter 5|sw5e-phb|5}).

entries.name: Training
entries: You can spend time between adventures learning a new language or training with a set of tools. Your GM might allow additional training options.
First, you must find an instructor willing to teach you. The GM determines how long it takes, and whether one or more {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} are required.
The training lasts for 250 days and costs 10 cr per day. After you spend the requisite amount of time and money, you learn the new language or gain proficiency with the new tool.

data.name: Chapter 9: Combat
entries: The shriek of {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} fire flying overhead. The {@i clash} of a gamorrean's axe striking against a composite {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}. The crackle of lightning emenating from a Sith lord's hands. The sharp tang of blood in the air, cutting through the stench of vile monsters. Roars of fury, shouts of triumph, cries of pain. Combat in D&D can be chaotic, deadly, and thrilling.

This chapter provides the rules you need for your characters and monsters to engage in combat, whether it is a brief skirmish or an extended conflict in a dungeon or on a field of battle. Throughout this chapter, the rules address you, the player or Game Master. The Game Master controls all the monsters and nonplayer characters involved in combat, and each other player controls an adventurer. "You" can also mean the character or monster that you control.

entries.name: The Order of Combat
entries: A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and force- or tech-casting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A {@b round} represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a {@b turn.} The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative}. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

entries.name: Surprise
entries: A band of adventurers sneaks up on a Mandalorian camp, springing from {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} to attack them. Kath hounds patrol down a hallway, leashed to their handler, unnoticed by the adventurers until the hound smells one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter until the end of their first turn.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

entries.name: Your Turn
entries: On your turn, you can move a distance up to your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} and take one action. You decide whether to move first or take your action first. Your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}—sometimes called your walking {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}—is noted on your character sheet.

The most common actions you can take are described in the {@book Actions in Combat|sw5e-phb|9|Actions in Combat} section later in this chapter. Many class features and other abilities provide additional options for your action.

entries.name: Combat Step By Step
entries: {@b 1. Determine surprise.} The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised. {@b 2. Establish positions.} The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are—how far away and in what direction. {@b 3. Roll initiative.} Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative}, determining the order of combatants' turns. {@b 4. Take turns.} Each participant in the battle takes a turn in {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} order. {@b 5. Begin the next round.} When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.
The {@book Movement and Position|sw5e-phb|9|Movement and Position} section later in this chapter gives the rules for your move.

You can forgo moving, taking an action, or doing anything at all on your turn. If you can't decide what to do on your turn, consider taking the Dodge or {@action Ready|sw5e-phb} action, as described in {@book Actions in Combat|sw5e-phb|9|Actions in Combat}

entries.name: Bonus Actions
entries: Various class features, powers, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}. The Cunning Action feature, for example, allows an operative to take a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}. You can take a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} only when a special ability, power, or other feature of the game states that you can do something as a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}. You otherwise don't have a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to take.
You can take only one {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} on your turn, so you must choose which {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to use when you have more than one available.

You choose when to take a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} during your turn, unless the {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}'s timing is specified, and anything that deprives you of your ability to take actions also prevents you from taking a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}.

entries.name: Object Interaction
entries: You can also interact with one object or feature of the environment at any time on your turn, even during your move or your action, as your object interaction. For example, you could open a door as you stride toward a foe, you could stow your weapon as you run, or you could grasp a two-handed weapon you are wielding in one hand with your other hand as you attack with it (releasing it requires no action).

If you want to interact with an additional object, you need to use your action or {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} (your choice). Some enhanced items and other special objects always require an action to use, as stated in their descriptions.

The GM might require you to use an action for any of these activities when it needs special care or when it presents an unusual obstacle. For instance, the GM could reasonably expect you to use an action to open a stuck door or turn a crank to lower a drawbridge.

entries.name: Other Activity on Your Turn
entries: Lastly, your turn can include a variety of flourishes that require neither your action nor your move.
You can communicate however you are able, through brief utterances and gestures, as you take your turn.

entries.name: Interacting with Objects Around You
entries: Here are a few examples of the sorts of thing you can do with your object interaction: - draw or stow a weapon - open or close a door - withdraw a stim from your pack - pick up a dropped weapon - take an item from a table - remove a ring from your finger - stuff some food into your mouth - plant a banner in the ground - fish a few chits from your belt pouch - drink all the beer in a glass - throw a lever or a switch - pull a glowstick from a sconce - take a book from a shelf you can reach - {@spell Extinguish|sw5e-phb|extinguish} a small flame - don a mask - pull the hood of your cloak up and over your head - put your ear to a door - turn a key in a lock - hand an item to another character

entries.name: Reactions
entries: Certain special abilities, powers, and situations allow you to take a special action called a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}. A {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, typically an instant response to a trigger of some kind, can occur on your turn or on someone else's. The {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, described later in this chapter, is the most common type of {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}.

When you take a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. If the {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} interrupts another creature's turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}.
Certain features, such as the scholar's Multitasker, might grant you an additional {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}. If you have two or more reactions, you can only take one per turn.

entries.name: Movement and Position
entries: In combat, characters and monsters are in constant motion, often using movement and position to gain the upper hand.

On your turn, you can move a distance up to your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. You can use as much or as little of your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} as you like on your turn, following the rules here.

Your movement can include jumping, climbing, and swimming. These different modes of movement can be combined with walking, or they can constitute your entire move. However you're moving, you deduct the distance of each part of your move from your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} until it is used up or until you are done moving.
The "Special Types of Movement" section in {@book Chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8} gives the particulars for jumping, climbing, and swimming.

entries.name: Actions That Grant Movement
entries: If an action, {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}, or {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} allows you to move as part of its effects, this additional movement does not count towards your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. If it does not require an action, however, it does count towards your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}.

entries.name: Breaking Up Your Move
entries: You can break up your movement on your turn, using some of your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} before and after your action. For example, if you have a {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 30 feet, you can move 10 feet, take your action, and then move 20 feet.

entries.name: Moving Between Attacks
entries: If you take an action that includes more than one {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack}, you can break up your movement even further by moving between those attacks. For example, a fighter with the Extra Attack feature who has a {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 25 feet could move 10 feet, attack, move 15 feet, and then attack again.

entries.name: Using Different Speeds
entries: If you have more than one {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}, such as your walking {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} and a flying {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}, you can switch back and forth between your speeds during your move. Whenever you switch, subtract the distance you've already moved from the new {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. The result determines how much farther you can move. If the result is 0 or less, you can't use the new {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} during the current move.

For example, if you have a flying {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 30 and a walking {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 40 because a Jedi cast the {@i burst of speed} power on you, you could walk 20 feet, then fly 10 feet, and then land to walk 10 feet more.

entries.name: Difficult Terrain
entries: Combat rarely takes place in bare rooms or on featureless plains. Boulder-strewn caverns, briar-choked forests, treacherous staircases—the setting of a typical fight contains {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

Every foot of movement in {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain} costs 1 extra foot. This rule is true even if multiple things in a space count as {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs are examples of {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}. The space of another creature, whether hostile or not, also counts as {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

entries.name: Being Prone
entries: Combatants often find themselves lying on the ground, either because they are knocked down or because they throw themselves down. In the game, they are {@condition Prone|sw5e-phb|prone}, a condition described in {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}.

You can {@b drop prone} without using any of your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. {@b Standing up} takes more effort, costing an amount of movement equal to half your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. For example, if your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} is 30 feet, you must spend 15 feet of movement to stand up. You can't stand up if you don't have enough movement left or if your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} is 0.

To move while {@condition Prone|sw5e-phb|prone}, you must {@b crawl} or use powers that teleport. Every foot of movement while crawling costs 1 extra foot. Crawling 1 foot in {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}, therefore, costs 3 feet of movement.

entries.name: Moving Around Other Creatures
entries: You can move through a nonhostile creature's space. In contrast, you can move through a hostile creature's space only if the creature is at least two sizes larger or smaller than you. Remember that another creature's space is {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain} for you.
Whether a creature is a friend or an enemy, you can't willingly end your move in its space.
If you leave a hostile creature's reach during your move, you provoke an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, as explained later in the chapter.

entries.name: Flying Movement
entries: Flying creatures enjoy many benefits of mobility, but they must also deal with the danger of falling. If a flying creature is knocked {@condition Prone|sw5e-phb|prone}, has its {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} reduced to 0, or is otherwise deprived of the ability to move, the creature falls, unless it has the ability to hover.

entries.name: Creature Size
entries: Each creature takes up a different amount of space. The Size Categories table shows how much space a creature of a particular size controls in combat. Objects sometimes use the same size categories.

entries.name: Space
entries: A creature's space is the area in feet that it effectively controls in combat, not an expression of its physical dimensions. A typical Medium creature isn't 5 feet wide, for example, but it does control a space that wide. If a Medium gamorrean stands in a 5-foot-wide doorway, other creatures can't get through unless the gamorrean lets them.

A creature's space also reflects the area it needs to fight effectively. For that reason, there's a limit to the number of creatures that can surround another creature in combat. Assuming Medium combatants, eight creatures can fit in a 5-foot radius around another one.

Because larger creatures take up more space, fewer of them can surround a creature. If five Large creatures crowd around a Medium or smaller one, there's little room for anyone else. In contrast, as many as twenty Medium creatures can surround a Gargantuan one.

If a square costs extra movement, as a square of {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain} does, you must have enough movement left to pay for entering it. For example, you must have at least 2 squares of movement left to enter a square of {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|sw5e-phb|difficult terrain}.

entries.name: Squeezing into a Smaller Space
entries: A creature can squeeze through a space that is large enough for a creature one size smaller than it. Thus, a Large creature can squeeze through a passage that's only 5 feet wide. While squeezing through a space, a creature must spend 1 extra foot for every foot it moves there, and it has {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. Attack rolls against the creature have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} while it's in the smaller space.

entries.name: Variant: Playing on a Grid
entries: If you play out a combat using a square grid and miniatures or other tokens, follow these rules. {@b {@i Squares.}} Each square on the grid represents 5 feet. {@b {@i Speed.}} Rather than moving foot by foot, move square by square on the grid. This means you use your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} in 5-foot segments. This is particularly easy if you translate your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} into squares by dividing the {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} by 5. For example, a {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 30 feet translates into a {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 6 squares. {@b {@i Entering a Square.}} To enter a square, you must have at least 1 square of movement left, unless the square is diagonally adjacent to the square you're in (discussed below). {@b {@i Corners.}} Diagonal movement can't cross the corner of a wall, large tree, or other terrain feature that fills its space. {@b {@i Ranges.}} To determine the range on a grid between two things—whether creatures or objects—start counting squares from a square adjacent to one of them and stop counting in the space of the other one. Count by the shortest route. {@b {@i Diagonals.}} When measuring range or moving diagonally, the first diagonal square counts as 5 feet, but the second diagonal square counts as 10 feet. This pattern of 5 feet and then 10 feet continues whenever you're counting diagonally, even if you move horizontally or vertically between different bits of diagonal movement. For instance, a character might move one square diagonally (5 feet), then three squares straight (15 feet), and then another square diagonally (10 feet) for a total movement of 30 feet.

entries.name: Actions in Combat
entries: When you take your action on your turn, you can take one of the actions presented here, an action you gained from your class or a special feature, or an action that you improvise. Many creatures have action options of their own in their stat blocks.
When you describe an action not detailed elsewhere in the rules, the GM tells you whether that action is possible and what kind of roll you need to make, if any, to determine success or failure.

entries.name: Attack
entries: The most common action to take in combat is the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, whether you are swinging a {@item Vibrosword|sw5e-phb|vibrosword}, firing a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true}, or brawling with your fists. With this action, you make one melee or ranged attack. See the "Making an Attack" section for the rules that govern attacks.
Certain features, such as the Extra Attack class feature, allow you to make more than one attack with this action.

entries.name: Cast a Power
entries: Force- and tech-casters such as consulars and engineers, as well as many creatures, have access to powers and can use them to great effect in combat. Each power has a casting time, which specifies whether the caster must use an action, a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, minutes, or even hours to cast the power. Casting a power is, therefore, not necessarily an action. Most powers do have a casting time of 1 action, so a force- or tech-caster often uses his or her action in combat to cast such a power. See {@book chapter 10|sw5e-phb|10} for the rules on force- and tech-casting.

entries.name: Dash
entries: When you take the {@action Dash|sw5e-phb} action, you gain extra movement for the current turn. The increase equals your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}, after applying any modifiers. With a {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 30 feet, for example, you can move up to 60 feet on your turn if you dash.

Any increase or decrease to your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} changes this additional movement by the same amount. If your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} of 30 feet is reduced to 15 feet, for instance, you can move up to 30 feet this turn if you Dash.

entries.name: Disengage
entries: If you take the {@action Disengage|sw5e-phb} action, your movement doesn't provoke {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks} for the rest of the turn.

entries.name: Dodge
entries: When you take the {@action Dodge|sw5e-phb} action, you focus entirely on avoiding attacks. Until the start of your next turn, any {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} made against you has {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} if you can see the attacker, and you make Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. You lose this benefit if you are {@condition Incapacitated|sw5e-phb} (as explained in {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}) or if your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} drops to 0.

entries.name: Guard
entries: You can defend an ally within 5 feet of you. When you take the {@action Guard|sw5e-phb} action, you focus entirely on preventing attacks from reaching your ally. Until the start of your next turn, any {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} made against the guarded ally has {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} if you can see the attacker, as long as the ally is within 5 feet of you.
Additionally, if an attack would hit the guarded ally, you can instead have it hit you (no action required). If you do so, the attacker chooses the maximum amount of damage instead of rolling.

entries.name: Help
entries: You can lend your aid to an ally in the completion of a task. When you take the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action, the ally you aid gains {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the next {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} it makes to perform the task you are helping with, provided that it makes the check before the start of your next turn.

Alternatively, you can aid an ally in attacking a creature within 5 feet of you. You feint, distract the target, or in some other way team up to make your ally's attack more effective. If your ally attacks the target before your next turn, the first {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} is made with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

entries.name: Hide
entries: When you take the {@action Hide|sw5e-phb} action, you make a Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|sw5e-phb}) check in an attempt to hide, following the rules in {@book chapter 7|sw5e-phb|7} for hiding. If you succeed, you gain certain benefits, as described in the {@book Unseen Attackers and Targets|sw5e-phb|9|Unseen Attackers and Targets} section later in this chapter.

entries.name: Improvising an Action
entries: Your character can do things not covered by the actions in this chapter, such as breaking down doors, intimidating enemies, sensing weaknesses in defenses, or calling for a parley with a foe. The only limits to the actions you can attempt are your imagination and your character's ability scores. See the descriptions of the ability scores in {@book chapter 7|sw5e-phb|7} for inspiration as you improvise. When you describe an action not detailed elsewhere in the rules, the GM tells you whether that action is possible and what kind of roll you need to make, if any, to determine success or failure.

entries.name: Ready
entries: Sometimes you want to get the jump on a foe or wait for a particular circumstance before you act. To do so, you can take the {@action Ready|sw5e-phb} action on your turn, which lets you act using your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} before the start of your next turn.

First, you decide what perceivable circumstance will trigger your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}. Then, you choose the action you will take in response to that trigger, or you choose to move up to your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} in response to it. Examples include "If the soldier steps on the trapdoor, I'll pull the lever that opens it," and "If the gamorrean steps next to me, I move away."

When the trigger occurs, you can either take your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} right after the trigger finishes or ignore the trigger. Remember that you can take only one {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} per round.

When you ready a power, you cast it as normal but hold its energy, which you release with your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} when the trigger occurs. To be readied, a power must have a casting time of 1 action, and holding onto the power's effect requires {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} (explained in {@book chapter 10|sw5e-phb|10}). If your {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} is broken, the power dissipates without taking effect. For example, if you are concentrating on the {@i knight speed} power and ready {@i shock,} your {@i knight speed} power ends, and if you take damage before you release {@i shock} with your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, your {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} might be broken.

entries.name: Search
entries: When you take the {@action Search|sw5e-phb} action, you devote your attention to finding something. Depending on the nature of your search, the GM might have you make a Wisdom ({@skill Perception|sw5e-phb}) check or an Intelligence ({@skill Investigation|sw5e-phb}) check.

entries.name: Use an Object
entries: Many objects and items, such as grenades or medpacs, require your action to use. When an object requires your action for its use, you take the {@action Use an Object|sw5e-phb} action. If you would normally have to use your object interaction to draw the item you are using, you can instead do so as part of the {@action Use an Object|sw5e-phb} action.

entries.name: Making an Attack
entries: Whether you're striking with a melee weapon, firing a weapon at range, or making an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} as part of a power, an attack has a simple structure.
{@b 1. Choose a target.} Pick a target within your attack's range: a creature, an object, or a location.

{@b 2. Determine modifiers.} The GM determines whether the target has {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} and whether you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} against the target. In addition, powers, special abilities, and other effects can apply penalties or bonuses to your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}.

{@b 3. Resolve the attack.} You make the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. On a hit, you roll damage, unless the particular attack has rules that specify otherwise. Some attacks cause special effects in addition to or instead of damage. If there's ever any question whether something you're doing counts as an attack, the rule is simple: if you're making an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, you're making an attack.

entries.name: Attack Rolls
entries: When you make an attack, your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} determines whether the attack hits or misses. To make an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, roll a {@dice d20} and add the appropriate modifiers. If the total of the roll plus modifiers equals or exceeds the target's {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb} (AC), the attack hits. The AC of a character is determined at character creation, whereas the AC of a creature is in its stat block.

entries.name: Modifiers to the Roll
entries: When a character makes an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, the two most common modifiers to the roll are an ability modifier and the character's {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. When a creature makes an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, it uses whatever modifier is provided in its stat block.

{@b {@i Ability Modifier.}} The ability modifier used for a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} is Strength, and the ability modifier used for a ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} is Dexterity. Weapons that have the finesse or thrown property break this rule.

Some powers also require an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. The ability modifier used for a power attack depends on the force- or tech-casting ability of the force- or tech-caster, as explained in {@book chapter 10|sw5e-phb|10}.

{@b {@i Proficiency Bonus.}} You add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} when you attack using a weapon with which you have proficiency, as well as when you attack with a power.

entries.name: Rolling 1 or 20
entries: Sometimes fate blesses or curses a combatant, causing the novice to hit and the veteran to miss.

If the {@dice d20} roll for an attack is a 20, the attack hits regardless of any modifiers or the target's AC. In addition, the attack is a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}, as explained later in this chapter.
If the {@dice d20} roll for an attack is a 1, the attack misses regardless of any modifiers or the target's AC.

entries.name: Choosing to be Hit
entries: Sometimes, an attack might miss you when you wanted it to hit. You can choose to allow a miss to hit you (no action required). If you do so, the attacker chooses the maximum amount of damage instead of rolling.

entries.name: Unseen Attackers and Targets
entries: Combatants often try to escape their foes' notice by hiding, casting the {@i force camouflage} power, or lurking in darkness.

When you attack a target that you can't see, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}. This is true whether you're guessing the target's location or you're targeting a creature you can hear but not see. If the target isn't in the location you targeted, you automatically miss, but the GM typically just says that the attack missed, not whether you guessed the target's location correctly.
When a creature can't see you, you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} against it.
If you are hidden—both unseen and unheard—when you make an attack, you give away your location when the attack hits or misses.

entries.name: Melee Attacks
entries: Used in hand-to-hand combat, a melee attack allows you to attack a foe within your reach. A melee attack typically uses a handheld weapon such as a {@item Vibrosword|sw5e-phb|vibrosword}, a lightsaber, or a {@item Vibrowhip|sw5e-phb|vibrowhip}. A typical monster makes a melee attack when it strikes with its claws, horns, teeth, tentacles, or other body part. A few powers also involve making a melee attack.

Most creatures have a 5-foot {@b reach} and can thus attack targets within 5 feet of them when making a melee attack. Certain creatures (typically those larger than Medium) have melee attacks with a greater reach than 5 feet, as noted in their descriptions.

Regardless of whether or not you are armed, you can fight in melee by making an unarmed strike. Your {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes} are a weapon with which you are proficient and, unless otherwise indicated, they do 1 + your Strength modifier kinetic damage.

entries.name: Opportunity Attacks
entries: In a fight, everyone is constantly watching for enemies to drop their guard. You can rarely move heedlessly past your foes without putting yourself in danger; doing so provokes an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}.

You can make an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} when a hostile creature that you can see moves out of your reach. To make the {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, you use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make one melee attack against the provoking creature. The attack interrupts the provoking creature's movement, occurring right before the creature leaves your reach.

You can avoid provoking an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} by taking the {@action Disengage|sw5e-phb} action. You also don't provoke an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} when you teleport or when someone or something unwillingly moves you without using your movement, action, {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}, or {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}. For example, you don't provoke an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} if an explosion hurls you out of a foe's reach or if gravity causes you to fall past an enemy. However, you do provoke an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} if a power such as {@i force jump}, or an ally's Formation fighting style feature, causes you to move out of an enemies' reach, unless that feature says otherwise.

entries.name: Grappling
entries: When you want to grab a creature or wrestle with it, you can use the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action to make a special melee attack, a {@b grapple}. If you're able to make multiple attacks with the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, this attack replaces one of them.

entries.name: Contests
entries: in Combat Battle often involves pitting your prowess against that of your foe. Such a challenge is represented by a contest. This section includes the most common contests that require an action in combat. The GM can use these contests as models for improvising others.

The target of your grapple must be no more than one size larger than you, and it must be within your reach. Using at least one free hand, which is occupied for the duration of the grapple, you try to seize the target by making a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check contested by the target's Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) or Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check (the target chooses the ability to use). If you succeed, you subject the target to the {@condition Grappled|sw5e-phb|grappled} condition (see {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}). The condition specifies the things that end it, and you can release the target whenever you like (no action required).

{@b {@i Escaping a Grapple.}} A {@condition Grappled|sw5e-phb|grappled} creature can use its action to escape. To do so, it must succeed on a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) or Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check contested by your Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check.

{@b {@i Moving a Grappled Creature.}} When you move, you can drag or carry the {@condition Grappled|sw5e-phb|grappled} creature with you, but your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} is halved, unless the creature is two or more sizes smaller than you.

entries.name: Shoving and Tripping
entries: Using the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, you can make a special melee attack to {@b shove} a creature to push it away from you, or to {@b trip} a creature to knock it prone. If you're able to make multiple attacks with the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, this attack replaces one of them.

The target of your shove or trip must be no more than one size larger than you, and it must be within your reach. You make a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) check contested by the target's Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) or Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check (the target chooses the ability to use). If you win the contest, you either shove the target 5 feet away from you or trip it prone.

entries.name: Ranged Attacks
entries: When you make a ranged attack, you fire a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true}, hurl a {@item Vibrodagger|sw5e-phb}, or otherwise strike a foe at a distance. A creature might have a natural ranged weapon. Many powers also involve making a ranged attack.

entries.name: Range
entries: You can make ranged attacks only against targets within a specified range. If a ranged attack, such as one made with a power, has a single range, you can't attack a target beyond this range. Some ranged attacks, such as those made with a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true}, have two ranges. The smaller number is the normal range, and the larger number is the long range. Your {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} has {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} when your target is beyond normal range, and you can't attack a target beyond the long range.

entries.name: Ranged Attacks in Close Combat
entries: Aiming a ranged attack is more difficult when a foe is next to you. When you make a ranged attack with a weapon, a power, or some other means, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} if you are within 5 feet of a hostile creature who can see you and who isn't {@condition Incapacitated|sw5e-phb}.

entries.name: Double-Weapon Fighting
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action and attack with a weapon with the light and double properties that you're wielding in two hands, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to attack with the other end of the weapon. You don't add your ability modifier to the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} of the bonus attack, unless that modifier is negative.

entries.name: Two-Weapon Fighting
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action and attack with a weapon with the light property that you're wielding in one hand, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to attack with a different light weapon that you're wielding in the other hand. You don't add your ability modifier to the damage roll of the bonus attack, unless that modifier is negative.
If a weapon has the thrown property, you can throw the weapon, instead of making a melee attack with it.

entries.name: Cover
entries: Walls, trees, creatures, and other obstacles can {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|provide cover} during combat, making a target more difficult to harm. A target can benefit from {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} only when an attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of the {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}.

There are four degrees of {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}. If a target is behind multiple sources of {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}, only the most protective degree of {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} applies, not added together.

A target with {@b one-quarter cover} has a +2 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. A target has one-quarter {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} if an obstacle blocks at least one-fourth of its body, such as a thin pillar or a creature of one size category smaller.

A target with {@b half cover} has a +3 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. A target has {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} if an obstacle blocks at least half of its body, such as a low wall or a creature of the same size category.

A target with {@b three-quarters cover} has a +5 bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}. A target has three-quarter {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} if about three-quarters of it is obstructed, whether by an obstacle or a creature of one size category larger.

A target with {@b total cover} can't be targeted directly by an attack or a power, although some powers can reach such a target by including it in an area of effect. A target has {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|total cover} if it is completely concealed by an obstacle.

entries.name: Variant: Creatures Providing Cover
entries: Sometimes, creatures in close proximity create a veritable mess of bodies, potentially causing attacks targeting one to hit another. Using this variant, if an attack would miss a creature by an amount less than or equal to the bonus to AC granted by the {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} of another creature, and the attack would hit that other creature, the GM might consider having that other creature take the attack's damage.

entries.name: Damage and Healing
entries: Injury and the risk of death are constant companions of those who explore the worlds of D&D. The thrust of a {@item Vibrosword|sw5e-phb|vibrosword}, a well-placed {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} shot, or a shock of lightning from a {@i shock} power all have the potential to damage, or even kill, the hardiest of creatures.

entries.name: Hit Points
entries: Hit points represent a combination of physical and mental durability, the will to live, and luck. Creatures with more {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} are more difficult to kill. Those with fewer {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} are more fragile.

A creature's current {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} (usually just called {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}) can be any number from the creature's hit point maximum down to 0. This number changes as a creature takes damage or receives healing.

Whenever a creature takes damage, that damage is subtracted from its {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. The loss of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} has no effect on a creature's capabilities until the creature drops to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.

entries.name: Damage Rolls
entries: Each weapon, power, and harmful monster ability specifies the damage it deals. You roll the damage die or dice, add any modifiers, and apply the damage to your target. Modified weapons, special abilities, and other factors can grant a bonus to damage.

When attacking with a {@b weapon,} you add your ability modifier—the same modifier used for the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}—to the damage. A {@b power} tells you which dice to roll for damage and whether to add any modifiers.

If a power or other effect deals damage to {@b more than one target} at the same time, roll the damage once for all of them. For example, when an engineer casts {@i explosion}, the power's damage is rolled once for all creatures caught in the blast.

entries.name: Critical Hits
entries: When you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}, you get to roll all of the attack's damage dice twice, including any additional damage dice, and add them together. Then add any relevant modifiers as normal. To {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} up play, you can roll all the damage dice at once.

{@b {@i Critical Hit Range.}} The {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range of an effect determines on what {@dice d20} results that effect scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}. Typically, an effect has a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range of 1, meaning it only scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} on a 20. A {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range of 2, however, would mean the effect scores a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} on a roll of 19 or 20. A {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range cannot exceed 5, scoring a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} on 16-20.

entries.name: Damage Types
entries: Different attacks, damaging powers, and other harmful effects deal different types of damage. Damage types have no rules of their own, but other rules, such as damage resistance, rely on the types.
The damage types follow, with examples to help a GM assign a damage type to a new effect.
{@b {@i Acid.}} Vials of corrosive liquid or the {@i acid splash} {@book tech power|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers} deal acid damage.
{@b {@i Cold.}} The chill energy of carbonite and cryogenesis deal cold damage.

{@b {@i Energy.}} Energy damage is the damage dealt by {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons, {@filter lightweapons|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon}, and other powers or abilities.
{@b {@i Fire.}} The concussive damage of an explosion or an open flame deal fire damage.
{@b {@i Force.}} Certain {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} that channel the pure energy of the Force deal force damage.

{@b {@i Ion.}} Ion damage is a special damage type that is most effective against droids and constructs. Simple electronics dealt ion damage are disabled until rebooted, unless that damage would destroy them outright.
{@b {@i Kinetic.}} Kinetic damage encompasses all physical damage commonly dealt by {@filter vibroweapons|items|type=martial weapon}.
{@b {@i Lightning.}} The electrifying energy of the {@i force lightning} power deals lightning damage.
{@b {@i Necrotic.}} Necrotic damage, dealt by powers like {@i death field}, withers matter and even the soul.
{@b {@i Poison.}} Venomous stings and the toxic {@i poison spray} power deal poison damage.
{@b {@i Psychic.}} The crippling agony causes by powers like {@i feedback} deal psychic damage.
{@b {@i Sonic.}} Debilitating noises cause sonic damage.
{@b {@i True.}} True damage is not dealt by any specific source. Instead, effects that prevent or redirect damage cannot be used to counter the loss of life caused by true damage.

entries.name: Damage Resistance and Vulnerability
entries: Some creatures and objects are exceedingly difficult or unusually easy to hurt with certain types of damage. If a creature or an object has resistance to a damage type, damage of that type is reduced by half against it. If a creature or an object has vulnerability to a damage type, damage of that type is doubled against it.

Multiple instances of resistance or vulnerability that affect the same damage type count as only one instance. For example, if a creature has resistance to lightning damage as well as resistance to all {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} damage, the damage of a {@i force lightning} is reduced by half, not reduced by three-quarters.

resistance and then vulnerability are applied after passive modifiers to damage, but before active modifiers. For example, a creature with resistance to kinetic damage, a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +4, and the Defense fighting mastery is hit by an attack that deals 22 kinetic damage. The 22 damage is first reduced by 4 and then halved, so the creature takes 9 damage. The creature also has the {@item Shield|sw5e-phb} fighting mastery, and uses its {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to further reduce the damage taken by 4, finally taking only 5 damage.

entries.name: Describing
entries: the Effects of Damage Game Masters describe hit point loss in different ways. When your current hit point total is above half your hit point maximum, you typically show no signs of injury. When you drop below half your hit point maximum, you show signs of wear, such as cuts and bruises. An attack that reduces you to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} strikes you directly, leaving a bleeding injury or other trauma, or it simply knocks you {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb}.

entries.name: Healing
entries: Unless it results in death, damage isn't permanent. Rest can restore a creature's {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} (as explained in {@book chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8}), and methods such as a {@i benevolence} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} or a {@item Medpac|sw5e-phb|medpac} can remove damage instantly.

When a creature receives healing of any kind, {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} regained are added to its current {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. A creature's {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} can't exceed its hit point maximum, so any {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} regained in excess of this number are lost. For example, a consular grants an operative 8 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} of healing. If the operative has 14 current {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} with a maximum of 20, the operative regains 6 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} from the consular, not 8.
A creature that has died can't regain {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} until a power such as {@i revitalize} has restored it to life.

entries.name: Hit Dice
entries: Resting (explained in {@book chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8}), as well as certain special traits such as the trandoshan's Regenerative, consume Hit Dice to restore {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. Whenever a creature rolls a Hit Die to restore {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, they add their Constitution modifier to the roll.

entries.name: Dropping to 0 Hit Points
entries: When you drop to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, you either die outright or fall {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb}, as explained in the following sections.

entries.name: Instant Death
entries: Massive damage can kill you instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and there is damage remaining, you die if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum.

For example, a consular with a maximum of 12 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} currently has 6 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. If she takes 18 damage from an attack, she is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, but 12 damage remains. Because the remaining damage equals her hit point maximum, the consular dies.

entries.name: Falling Unconscious
entries: If damage reduces you to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and fails to kill you, you fall {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb} (see {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}). This unconsciousness ends if you regain any {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.

entries.name: Death Saving Throws
entries: Whenever you start your turn with 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, you must make a special {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, called a {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw}, to determine whether you creep closer to death or hang onto life. Unlike other {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}, this one isn't tied to any ability score. You are in the hands of fate now, aided only by powers and features that improve your chances of succeeding on a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. Roll a {@dice d20}. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect by itself. On your third success, you become stable (see below). On your third failure, you die. The successes and failures don't need to be consecutive; keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. The number of both is reset to zero when you regain any {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} or become stable.

{@b {@i Rolling 1 or 20.}} When you make a {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} and roll a 1 on the {@dice d20}, it counts as two failures. If you roll a 20 on the {@dice d20}, you regain 1 hit point.

{@b {@i Damage at 0 Hit Points.}} If you take any damage while you have 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} (for example, by catching fire because your limbs were all chopped off next to a pit of lava), you suffer a {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} failure. If the damage is from a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit}, you suffer two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds your hit point maximum, you suffer instant death.

entries.name: Stabilizing a Creature
entries: The best way to save a creature with 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} is to heal it. If healing is unavailable, the creature can at least be stabilized so that it isn't killed by a failed {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw}.

You can use your action to administer first aid to an {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb} creature and attempt to stabilize it, which requires a successful DC 10 Wisdom ({@skill Medicine|sw5e-phb}) check, or an Intelligence ({@skill Technology|sw5e-phb}) check for a droid or construct.

A {@b stable} creature doesn't make {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throws}, even though it has 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, but it does remain {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb}. The creature stops being stable, and must start making {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throws} again, if it takes any damage. A stable creature that isn't healed regains 1 hit point after 1d4 hours.

entries.name: Monsters and Death
entries: Most GMs have a monster die the instant it drops to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, rather than having it fall {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb} and make {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throws}.
Mighty villains and special nonplayer characters are common exceptions; the GM might have them fall {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb} and follow the same rules as player characters.

entries.name: Knocking a Creature Out
entries: Sometimes an attacker wants to incapacitate a foe, rather than deal a killing blow. When an attacker reduces a creature to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} with a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack}, or {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon that deals ion or energy damage, the attacker can knock the creature out. The attacker can make this choice the instant the damage is dealt. The creature falls {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb} and is stable.

entries.name: Temporary Hit Points
entries: Some powers and special abilities confer temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} to a creature. Temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} aren't actual {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}; they are a buffer against damage, a pool of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} that protect you from injury.

When you have temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and take damage, the temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} are lost first, and any leftover damage carries over to your normal {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. For example, if you have 5 temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and take 7 damage, you lose the temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and then take 2 damage.

Because temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} are separate from your actual {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, they can exceed your hit point maximum. A character can, therefore, be at full {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and receive temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.

Healing can't restore temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, and they can't be added together. If you have temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and receive more of them, you decide whether to keep the ones you have or to gain the new ones. For example, if a power grants you 12 temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} when you already have 10, you can have 12 or 10, not 22.

If you have 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, receiving temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} doesn't restore you to consciousness or stabilize you. They can still absorb damage directed at you while you're in that state, but only true healing can save you.
Unless a feature that grants you temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} has a duration, they last until they're depleted or you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: Temporary Force and Tech Points
entries: Similar to temporary {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, some powers, abilities, or features grant temporary force or tech points to a creature. When you would expend force or tech points—whether through a power, ability, or feature—the temporary points are spent first.
You can only have one source of temporary force or tech points. If you have temporary force or tech points and receive more of them, you decide whether to keep the ones you have or gain the new ones.
Unless a feature that grants you temporary force or tech points has a duration, they last until they're depleted or you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: Underwater Combat
entries: When adventurers pursue karkarodons back to their undersea domain, fight off gungans in an ancient shipwreck, or find themselves in a flooded dungeon room, they must fight in a challenging environment. Underwater the following rules apply.

When making a {@b melee weapon attack,} a creature that doesn't have a swimming {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} (either natural or granted by a power) has {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} unless the weapon is a {@item Vibrodagger|sw5e-phb} or {@item Vibrospear|sw5e-phb}.
A {@b ranged weapon attack} automatically misses a target beyond the weapon's normal range, but functions normally against a target within normal range.
Creatures and objects that are fully immersed in water have resistance to fire damage.

entries.name: Mounted Combat
entries: A trooper charging into battle on a dewback, an engineer casting powers from the seat of a speeder, or a consular soaring through the sky on shuttle all enjoy the benefits of {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} and mobility that a mount can provide.
An appropriately sized vehicle or a willing creature that is at least one size larger than you and that has an appropriate anatomy can serve as a mount, using the following rules.

entries.name: Mounting and Dismounting
entries: Once during your move, you can mount or dismount a vehicle or willing creature that is within 5 feet of you. Doing so costs an amount of movement equal to half your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed}. For example, if your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} is 30 feet, you must spend 15 feet of movement to mount a dewback. Therefore, you can't mount it if you don't have 15 feet of movement left or if your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} is 0.

If an effect moves your mount against its will while you're on it, you must succeed on a DC 10 Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} or fall off the mount, landing prone in a space within 5 feet of it. If you're knocked {@condition Prone|sw5e-phb|prone} while mounted, you must make the same {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}.

If your mount is knocked {@condition Prone|sw5e-phb|prone}, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to dismount it as it falls and land on your feet. Otherwise, you are dismounted and fall {@condition Prone|sw5e-phb|prone} in a space within 5 feet it.

entries.name: Controlling a Mount
entries: While you're mounted, you have two options. You can either control the mount or allow it to act independently. Intelligent creatures act independently.

You can control a mount only if it has been trained to accept a rider. Domesticated animals, such as dewbacks or kaadu, and similar creatures are assumed to have such training. The {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} of a controlled mount changes to match yours when you mount it. It moves as you direct it, and it has only three action options: Dash, Disengage, and Dodge. A controlled mount can move and act even on the turn that you mount it. All vehicles are considered controlled mounts, unless a feature says otherwise.

An independent mount retains its place in the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} order. Bearing a rider puts no restrictions on the actions the mount can take, and it moves and acts as it wishes. It might flee from combat, rush to attack and devour a badly injured foe, or otherwise act against your wishes.
In either case, if the mount provokes an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} while you're on it, the attacker can target you or the mount.

data.name: Chapter 10: Force- and Tech-casting
entries: Magic exists in the worlds of {@i Star Wars} in the form of powers. This chapter provides the rules for casting these powers. There are two major sources of these power: the Force and technology. While multiple classes use the Force or technology to fuel their powers, there are only the two sources. Regardless, powers follow the rules here.

entries.name: What is a Power?
entries: A power is a discrete enhanced effect, a single shaping of the energies of the Force or a result of a technological formula, that creates a desired effect. In casting a power, a character carefully constructs the desired effect using the source of their power, and then releases it, all in the span of seconds.

Powers can be versatile tools, weapons, or protective wards. They can deal damage or undo it, impose or remove conditions (see {@book Appendix A|sw5e-phb|14}), {@spell Drain Life|sw5e-phb|drain life} energy away, and restore life to the dead.

A great number of powers exist, and over time many have been created and forgotten. An ancient {@spell Force Technique|sw5e-phb|force technique} may exist in a long-lost {@item Holocron|sw5e-phb|holocron}, or a piece of Rakatan schemata may contain revolutionary tech.

entries.name: Power Level
entries: Every power has a level from 0 to 9. A power's level is a general indicator of how powerful it is, with the lowly {@i burst of speed} at 1st level and the powerful {@i greater explosion} at 9th. At-will powers—simple but effective powers that characters can cast almost by rote—are level 0. The higher a power's level, the higher level a force- or tech-caster must be to use that power.
Power level and character level don't correspond directly. Typically, a character has to be at least 17th level, not 9th level, to cast a 9th-level power.

entries.name: Known Powers
entries: Before a force- or tech-caster can use a power, he or she must have the power learned, or must have access to the power in an enhanced item. Once a power is learned, it is always prepared. The number of powers a caster can have at any given time depends on the character's level.

When you learn a power, either an at-will, 1st-level, or higher, you choose from the list of powers provided in {@book chapter 11|sw5e-phb|11} and {@book chapter 12|sw5e-phb|12}. You can learn powers from any level up to your Max Power Level, including at-will powers. The total number of powers you learn in this way can't exceed your Force or {@book Tech Powers Known|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers} for your class.

If a power is granted to you by a class feature, that power does not count against your powers known and you can't voluntarily unlearn it. If you already know that power, you may learn an additional power that is available to you.

Additionally, every time you learn a new power as a result of gaining a level, you can choose one of the powers you know and replace it with another power of the same type, as long as that power is not of a higher level than your Max Power Level.

entries.name: Force and Tech Points
entries: Regardless of how many powers a caster knows or prepares, he or she can cast only a limited number of powers before resting. Manipulating the Force and channeling its energy into even a simple power is physically and mentally taxing, and higher-level powers are even more so. Thus, each casting class's description includes a table showing how many force or tech points a character can use at each character level. For example, the 3rd-level consular Umara with 17 Wisdom has 15 force points.

When a character casts a power, he or she expends a number of points based on the level of the power to create the slot to cast it. At-will powers always cost 0 points, while casting a power at any other level costs the power level + 1 points, as shown in the Power Level Point Cost table below. When Umara casts {@i project}, a 1st-level power, she spends two of her 12 force points, leaving 10 remaining.

Finishing a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} restores any expended force points, and finishing a short or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} restores any expended tech points (see {@book chapter 8|sw5e-phb|8} for the rules on resting).

entries.name: Casting
entries: in Armor Because of the mental focus and precise gestures required for force- and tech-casting, you must be proficient with the armor you are wearing to cast a power. You are otherwise too distracted and hampered by your armor for force- or tech-casting.

entries.name: Casting a Power at a Higher Level
entries: When a caster casts a power using at a higher level than the power's normal level, the power assumes the higher level for that casting. For instance, if Umara casts {@i project} at 2nd-level, she uses three force points and that {@i project} is 2nd level.
Many powers have more powerful effects when cast at a higher level, as indicated in the {@b {@i Force Potency}} and {@b {@i Overcharge Tech}} sections of the power's description

entries.name: At-Will Powers
entries: An at-will power is one that can be cast without expending force or tech points. An at-will power's level is 0.

entries.name: Casting Focuses
entries: While {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} doesn't require a focus to cast {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} requires that you have a tech focus in order to cast {@book tech powers|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}.

entries.name: Casting a Power
entries: When a character casts any power, the same basic rules are followed, regardless of the character's class or the power's effects.

Each power description in {@book chapter 11|sw5e-phb|11} and {@book chapter 12|sw5e-phb|12} begins with a block of information, including the power's name, level, alignment (for {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}), prerequisites (if it has any), casting time, range, and duration. The rest of a power entry describes the power's effect.

entries.name: Power Alignments
entries: Most {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} are aligned with one of the opposing sides of the Force—light and dark—while many fall somewhere in the middle—universal. You use your Wisdom for {@book light side powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, Charisma for {@book dark side powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, and Wisdom or Charisma for {@book universal powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} (your choice). Additionally, certain archetypes and feats offer benefits to using powers of a specific alignment.

entries.name: Prerequisites
entries: Certain {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} are built as more powerful version of previous powers. They require that you know the previous power before you can learn the new one, and you must retain knowledge of the previous power to be able to cast the new one. If you are learning two or more powers at the same time, you can learn a power at the same time that you learn its prerequisites.
For instance, to learn the {@i knight speed} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} you would first need to learn the {@i burst of speed} power, as indicated by its prerequisites.

entries.name: Casting Time
entries: Most powers require a single action to cast, but some powers require a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}, a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, or much more time to cast.

entries.name: Bonus Action
entries: A power cast with a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} is especially swift. You can only cast one 1st-level or higher power using your action or {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} on each of your turns. Once you've done so, you can only cast at-will powers with your action or {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} on this turn.

entries.name: Reactions
entries: Some powers can be cast as reactions. These powers take a fraction of a second to bring about and are cast in response to some event. If a power can be cast as a {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, the power's description tells you exactly when you can do so.

entries.name: Longer Casting Times
entries: Certain powers require more time to cast: minutes or even hours. When you cast a power with a casting time longer than a single action or {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, you must spend your action each turn casting the power, and you must maintain your {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} while you do so (see "{@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb}" below). If your {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} is broken, the power fails, but you don't expend force or tech points. If you want to try casting the power again, you must start over.

entries.name: Range
entries: The target of a power must be within the power's range. For a power like {@i shock}, the target is a creature. For a power like {@i explosion}, the target is the point in space where the explosion occurs.

Most powers have ranges expressed in feet. Some power can target only a creature (including you) that you touch. Other powers, such as the {@i shield} power, affect only you. These powers have a range of self.

Powers that create cones or lines of effect that originate from you also have a range of self, indicating that the origin point of the power's effect must be you (see {@book Areas of Effect|sw5e-phb|10|Areas of Effect} later in this chapter).
Once a power is cast, its effects aren't limited by its range, unless the power's description says otherwise.

entries.name: Duration
entries: A power's duration is the length of time the power persists. A duration can be expressed in rounds, minutes, hours, or even years. Some powers specify that their effects last until the powers are dispelled or destroyed.

entries.name: Instantaneous
entries: Many powers are instantaneous. The power harms, heals, creates, or alters a creature or an object in a way that can't be dispelled, because its effect exists only for an instant.

entries.name: Concentration
entries: Some powers require you to maintain {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} in order to keep their effect active. If you lose {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}, such a power ends.

If a power must be maintained with {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}, that fact appears in its Duration entry, and the power specifies how long you can concentrate on it. You can end {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} at any time (no action required).

Normal activity, such as moving and attacking, doesn't interfere with {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}. The following factors can break {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}:

The GM might also decide that certain environmental phenomena, such as {@spell Turbulence|sw5e-phb|turbulence} on a ship or rocky terrain on a speeder, require you to succeed on a DC 10 Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} to maintain {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} on a power.

items: {@b Casting another power that requires concentration.} You lose {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} on a power if you cast another power that requires {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}. You can't concentrate on two powers at once.

{@b Taking damage.} Whenever you take damage while you are concentrating on a power, you must make a Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} to maintain your {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration}. The DC equals 10 or half the damage you take, whichever number is higher. If you take damage from multiple sources, such as a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} shot and a {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, you make a separate {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} for each source of damage.
{@b Being incapacitated or killed.} You lose {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} on a power if you are {@condition Incapacitated|sw5e-phb} or if you die.

entries.name: Targets
entries: A typical power requires you to pick one or more targets to be affected by the power's effect. A power's description tells you whether the power targets creatures, objects, or a point of origin for an area of effect (described below). Unless a power has a perceptible effect, a creature might not know it was targeted by a power at all. An effect like crackling lightning is obvious, but a more subtle effect, such as an attempt to read a creature's thoughts, typically goes unnoticed, unless a power says otherwise.

entries.name: A Clear Path to the Target
entries: To target something, you must have a clear path to it, so it can't be behind {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|total cover}.

If you place an area of effect at a point that you can't see and an obstruction, such as a wall, is between you and that point, the point of origin comes into being on the near side of that obstruction.

entries.name: Targeting Yourself
entries: If a power targets a creature of your choice, you can choose yourself, unless the creature must be hostile or specifically a creature other than you. If you are in the area of effect of a power you cast, you can target yourself.

entries.name: Areas of Effect
entries: Powers such as {@i force storm} and {@i explosion} {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} an area, allowing them to affect multiple creatures at once.

A power's description specifies its area of effect, which typically has one of five different shapes: cone, cube, cylinder, line, or sphere. Every area of effect has a point of origin, a location from which the power's effect erupts. The rules for each shape specify how you position its {@b point of origin}. Typically, a point of origin is a point in space, but some powers have an area whose origin is a creature or an object.

A power's effect expands in straight lines from the point of origin. If no unblocked straight line extends from the point of origin to a location within the area of effect, that location isn't included in the power's area. To block one of these imaginary lines, an obstruction must provide {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|total cover}, as explained in {@book chapter 9|sw5e-phb|9}.

entries.name: Cone
entries: A cone extends in a direction you choose from its point of origin. A cone's width at a given point along its length is equal to that points distance from the point of origin. A cone's area of effect specifies its maximum length.
A cone's point of origin is not included in the cones area of effect, unless you decide otherwise.

entries.name: Cube
entries: You select a cube's point of origin, which lies anywhere on a face of the cubic effect. The cube's size is expressed as the length of each side.
A cube's point of origin is not included in the cube's area of effect, unless you decide otherwise.

entries.name: Cylinder
entries: A cylinder's point of origin is the center of a circle of a particular radius, as given in the power description. The circle must either be on the ground or at the height of the power effect. The energy in a cylinder expands in straight lines from the point of origin to the perimeter of the circle, forming the base of the cylinder. The power's effect then shoots up from the base or down from the top, to a distance equal to the height of the cylinder.
A cylinder's point of origin is included in the cylinder's area of effect.

entries.name: Line
entries: A line extends from its point of origin in a straight path up to its length and covers an area defined by its width. A line's point of origin is not included in the line's area of effect, unless you decide otherwise.

entries.name: Sphere
entries: You select a sphere's point of origin, and the sphere extends outward from that point. The sphere's size is expressed as a radius in feet that extends from the point.
A sphere's point of origin is included in the sphere's area of effect.

entries.name: Saving Throws
entries: Many powers specify that a target can make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} to avoid some or all of a power's effects. The power specifies the ability that the target uses for the save and what happens on a success or failure.
